He builds AI chatbots that answer from your own documents, Python backend APIs, and computer vision and speech models. He also takes select freelance AI and backend projects alongside his full-time job.

# Freelance AI chatbot developer for document assistants
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/services/llm-rag-development/
Hire a freelance AI chatbot developer in Mumbai. Chatbots that answer from your own documents, show their sources and say "I do not know" when unsure.

As a freelance AI chatbot developer, I build Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbots that answer from your own documents. Every answer shows its source, and when the documents do not contain the answer, the chatbot says so instead of guessing. The method is called RAG (retrieval-augmented generation). You receive a working service, a simple chat screen, tests and handover notes.

Who it is for: Support and operations leads: Staff and customers keep asking questions whose answers already sit in manuals and policy files. A chatbot that answers from those files and shows its source spares people the search, and anyone can check the answer. Founders adding an AI feature: You want a chatbot or assistant inside a product or website. A working prototype on your own content shows real answer quality early, before you decide how much to build. Compliance and HR teams: Policies change and exact wording matters. You need each answer tied to the document it came from, and a plain "not found" when the policy says nothing on the question. Teams with a customer chat channel: Customers already write to you on WhatsApp or in an app. You need AI replies that do not keep them waiting, a saved history of each conversation and alerts for human operators.

Problems I solve: Nobody can tell where an answer came from. Each reply names the source document, shows the passage it relied on and carries a confidence label. A reviewer checks the claim against that passage instead of trusting the chatbot's wording. The bot misreads what the user is asking for. I design flows around what the user wants. A simple router sends document questions, booking requests and small talk to different handlers, and chat history lives in a database. In client chatbot work this reduced failures during complex bookings. A hosted AI model is retired or slows down. Model names and fallback order live in settings, so the service switches to a backup model without a code change, and each reply states which model answered. Request IDs plus metrics and traces, as built in my Traceable AI Backend, make a silent switch visible. You cannot tell if a change made answers better or worse. I keep a list of questions with the expected answers, including ones the documents should not answer. My healthcare example has such a list, checked by hand; for a client I add automatic scoring on every change. Visitors try to trick or flood the chatbot. On the scam honeypot I added a filter for prompt-injection attempts (messages that try to override the AI's instructions) and a request limit of 1 per second per visitor, with bursts of 5. For a client I would add a test set of attacks.

Deliverables: A working chatbot service with clear instructions for connecting to it (an API); Your documents prepared so the chatbot finds the right passage; Safety checks that block weak or off-topic answers; A source and a confidence label on every answer; A simple chat screen (Streamlit or React) for demos and review; Tests, setup notes and a handover walkthrough.

What I need from you: Some of your real documents, awkward ones with tables or images included, so passage search can be tested on real material.; A list of real questions your users ask, the answers you would accept, and a few questions the documents should not be able to answer.; Who may see which documents, and where text may go: an online AI service, your cloud account or your own servers.; Where the chatbot will live, such as a website, an app, WhatsApp or an internal tool, and a technical contact for that system..

Technology: FastAPI and Pydantic (Serve the chatbot through an API, check every request, and keep thresholds and model names in settings files.); sentence-transformers (Turns passages and questions into numbers that capture meaning, so the closest passages can be found. Runs on a standard processor (CPU).); ChromaDB (Stores those numbers on disk and returns the closest passages for each question.); AI model APIs (Groq, OpenAI) (The language model that writes each answer from the passages it is given, with backup models if one fails.); Local AI models (Ollama, vLLM) (Used instead of an online service when documents and prompts must stay on your own servers.); PostgreSQL and Supabase (Keep chat history and user profiles, so a bot can remember each conversation.); Redis and Celery (Run slow AI replies in the background, so a chat channel such as WhatsApp is not blocked while the AI works.); Streamlit or React (Provide the simple chat screen where reviewers see the answer, its source passage and the confidence label.); Docker and pytest (Docker packages the service so it runs the same anywhere. pytest runs the automatic checks after each change.).

Trade-offs: Online AI service or your own servers. Online services such as Groq or OpenAI are quick to start. Hosting the model on your own servers keeps every document and prompt in-house but needs a stronger machine. I usually prototype on non-sensitive samples, then decide with you. Strict answers or more answers. A high match score gives more "not found" replies and fewer wrong answers. A low score answers more questions but risks mistakes. For policy, health or finance content I suggest starting strict and loosening only after testing real questions. Remember the conversation or not. Memory lets a user ask a follow-up, but it needs stored history, privacy rules and more testing. My healthcare example answers each question on its own. For customer chat I store history in a database. I add memory only when the use case needs it.

Where it fits: Clinic and hospital administration: Front-desk and billing staff ask about discharge, refills, insurance and visit rules. A chatbot over the facility's own policies answers with the source and declines to guess on medical questions. HR and internal help desks: Employees ask the same questions about leave, expenses and onboarding. An assistant that answers from the current policy files and names the file keeps HR in control of what it says. Software companies with a help centre: Customers search long help articles. An assistant inside the product answers from those articles, shows which article it used and says so when the help centre has no answer. Service businesses that sell on WhatsApp: Customers ask about bookings, orders and returns at any hour. AI replies sent in the background, a saved conversation history and alerts for a human operator keep the chat moving.

Q: What is a RAG chatbot? A: A RAG chatbot looks up the right passages in your own documents first and only then writes its answer from them. RAG stands for retrieval-augmented generation. Because the answer is built from your documents, it can show its source. It can also say "not found" when the documents do not cover the question, instead of guessing.

Q: How do you stop a chatbot from making things up? A: With several layers, not one instruction. First the chatbot checks that the documents really contain the answer. Weak matches never reach the AI language model (LLM), the part that writes the reply. A fixed fallback sentence covers the rest. In my healthcare example, out-of-scope questions get a plain "not found" instead of a guess.

Q: Can a chatbot run on my own servers? A: Often, yes. At work I build on AI models hosted on the client's own servers, so no data or prompts leave the building. My personal projects use online services such as Groq. During planning we choose what fits your privacy needs, budget and answer quality.

Q: How much does an AI chatbot cost for a website? A: I do not publish a price list, because chatbots vary a lot. The cost depends on how many documents you have, how they are organised, where the chatbot must run and how much testing you need. After reading your brief I suggest a fixed price or hourly billing. We agree it in writing before I start.

Q: What kinds of documents can the chatbot use? A: Text-based documents such as policies, manuals, circulars and support articles. Tables and images inside documents can be harder, so we test those early. I start with a small sample of yours to check how well the chatbot finds the right passages, before we commit to the full build.

Q: Can my team maintain it after you finish? A: That is the aim. Instructions and adjustable settings live in simple settings files, and the code has tests. The handover includes a walkthrough of how to add documents and tune the settings. If you want ongoing help, we can agree a maintenance period in writing.

Q: What happens when our documents change? A: The search index is rebuilt from the updated files. In my healthcare example, an ingest step can wipe and rebuild the index, and identical passages are not stored twice. It does not yet watch for file changes or keep old versions apart. For a client I would add both, so outdated wording cannot answer a new question.

Q: Does the chatbot need training on our documents? A: No training run is needed. When a question arrives, the chatbot searches your documents for the best passages, so updating it means changing the files and refreshing the search index, not retraining a model. In my language model projects, quality came from retrieval, checks and prompts, not from training a model.

# Document data extraction with AI
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/services/ai-document-compliance-automation/
Freelance document AI: tools that read PDFs and forms and pull out clean data, with a quote from the source for each fact and checks on AI drafts.

I build document data extraction with AI: tools that read PDFs, forms and reports and turn them into clean, checkable data. Every extracted fact links back to the exact quote in your document. When AI writes a draft, code checks it against the original notes. I measure accuracy on your own files.

Who it is for: Compliance and risk teams: You read long circulars, permits and regulations to list the duties in them. You need a list where every duty links to the exact passage, so a reviewer can verify each one quickly. Internal audit teams: Findings start as short checklist notes. You want clear first drafts, in bulk when needed, with checks in code that block any figure, date or owner the auditor did not write. Reporting and data teams: Answers sit in a very large database that few people can query. You want plain questions turned into queries, plus an accuracy test that runs them, so you know how far to trust the results. Product teams adding AI to an app: You run a live product and want drafting or extraction added without rebuilding it. A separate service with a clear data agreement can be updated on its own.

Problems I solve: AI page numbers and citations cannot be trusted. The AI copies out the sentence it relied on; code finds it in the PDF and reads the page from the document. The AI's own page numbers were wrong 56% of the time; now 97.2% of 1,266 production records link to an exact passage. AI drafts include figures, dates or names nobody wrote. Code compares each draft with the source note and rejects it if it adds a figure, date or owner. On the audit drafting service, 0 invented facts were found across 27 checked draft versions. Nobody knows how accurate the output really is. I build the scoring step first and run it on a sample of your documents. On the database project, simple scoring suggested about 93% quality, but running the queries showed a far lower true figure. Long documents are too big to read in one go. I split the document at page boundaries, extract from each piece and rejoin duties that cross a break. I also measure where processing time goes: the changes that helped cut a six-document benchmark from 80.4 to 60.0 minutes. A new AI tool must fit the product you already run. I build it as a separate FastAPI service with a clear data contract: an agreed shape for what it sends and receives. The audit service was connected to an existing Spring Boot and React product, and the client adopted it the day after handover.

Deliverables: A service that reads your documents and returns clean, structured data; Evidence links: each fact tied to the exact quote it came from; Automatic checks that reject AI-written text containing invented details; Bulk processing for spreadsheets or whole folders of documents; A scoring tool that measures accuracy on a sample of your own documents; A review screen or export (web page or spreadsheet), if you need one.

What I need from you: Examples of the documents you handle, awkward ones included, and a list of the facts you want pulled from each.; A small set of correct answers: documents your team has already read and marked up by hand, which I use to score accuracy.; Where documents may be processed (your servers, your cloud account or an online AI service) and any privacy rules that apply.; How reviewers work today, such as spreadsheets or an existing product, so the output fits their routine and approval steps..

Technology: FastAPI and Pydantic (Serve the extraction service as an API and check every result against an agreed shape, such as allowed categories.); PyMuPDF (Opens PDFs and finds where a quoted passage sits, so the page number and highlight come from the document, not the AI.); Local AI models (Ollama, vLLM) (Read the text and return structured fields, hosted on your own servers so documents and prompts stay in-house.); TF-IDF similarity search (A word-weighting method that finds similar past examples, such as earlier findings, to show the AI how your team writes.); React and pdf.js (Show the PDF beside the extracted list with the evidence highlighted, so a reviewer can check each item against its source.); SQL databases (Oracle) (Used by the accuracy test: each generated query is run for real, and its rows are checked against a known-correct query.); pytest and scoring scripts (Run automatic tests, and score the output against correct answers from your documents after every change.); Docker (Packages the service with its settings, so your team can run it on its own machines the same way I do.).

Trade-offs: Find every item or only sure ones. Tuning to catch every item raises recall (the share of items found) but adds wrong extras. Tuning for certainty raises precision (the share of found items that are correct) but misses items. I ask which mistake costs you more, then report both on your documents. Bigger AI model or faster answers. A larger model may read more carefully but is slower and needs a stronger machine. I compare candidate models on your documents against a time limit you set, as I did with four models on the audit drafting service. Fully automatic or reviewed by a person. For compliance and audit work I keep a person in charge. Each item links to its source, and a reviewer can accept, edit or reject it. Full automation only suits low-risk fields where accuracy has been measured.

Where it fits: Bank compliance teams: A new regulator circular arrives. The team needs the duties in it listed and sorted into fixed categories, each tied to the exact passage for review. Site and plant compliance managers: Environmental permits and licences set conditions a site must meet. A tool can list each condition with its clause, so reviewers can check every one against the source. Internal audit and risk teams: A long checklist workbook needs a first-draft finding for every row. Bulk drafting with invented-detail checks gives reviewers one grid to approve, change or reject row by row. Finance and operations reporting teams: Business users wait on analysts for database reports. Plain questions turned into queries, with an accuracy test that runs them, show the team how far to trust the results.

Q: What is document AI? A: Document AI is software that reads documents such as PDFs, forms and reports. It turns what they say into structured data you can search, check and use. It can pull out names, dates, amounts and obligations. I build it so every extracted fact links back to the exact quote in the source document.

Q: How much does document AI cost? A: It depends on the number and variety of your documents, the accuracy you need and where the tool must run. I do not publish a price list. After a short brief and a test on a sample of your files, I suggest a fixed price or hourly billing. We agree it in writing before I start.

Q: How accurate is AI data extraction from PDFs? A: Accuracy is measured on your own files and reported plainly. I build a scoring tool that compares the output with a small set of correct answers from your documents, then fix the mistakes it finds. On a regulatory project, 97.2% of 1,266 production records link to an exact passage; that measures traceability, not completeness.

Q: Can my documents stay on our own servers? A: Yes, and that is a common requirement. Several systems I work on use AI models hosted on the client's own servers, so documents, prompts and usage records stay on the machine. During planning we check what hardware is available, because larger models need stronger machines.

Q: How do you stop AI from adding invented details? A: With checks in code, not just instructions in a prompt. In the audit drafting service I built, any figure, date or owner that is not in the source note causes the draft to be rejected automatically. In 27 checked draft versions, a small sample, I found no invented facts. A reviewer still accepts, edits or rejects every draft.

Q: Can this connect to our existing product? A: Yes. I connected an AI drafting service to a live product built with Spring Boot and React. It runs as a separate FastAPI service. There is a clear agreement about the data it sends and receives. The main product and the new service can be updated separately.

Q: Will the AI find every item in a long document? A: No. In a controlled comparison on documents held back from tuning, recall (how many of the real obligations were found) rose from 32% to 69% on Basel III rules and from 69% to 82% on KYC (know-your-customer) rules. Some are still missed, so every result links to its source and a person reviews the list.

Q: Can it read scanned pages and invoices? A: PDFs that already contain typed text are the easiest. Scanned pages and photos first need text recognition (OCR), and results depend on scan quality, so I test a sample of your scans before agreeing a plan. My case studies here cover regulatory PDFs, audit notes and a database, not invoices.

# Hire a FastAPI developer for Python backends and APIs
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/services/ai-backend-fastapi-django/
Hire a freelance FastAPI and Django developer in Mumbai. Python backend APIs with PostgreSQL, Docker, automated tests and logs for fast debugging.

Hire a FastAPI developer for the behind-the-scenes software (a backend API) that lets your website, app or Artificial Intelligence (AI) feature work with your data. I write it in Python with FastAPI or Django, store data in PostgreSQL and package it with Docker. I add automated tests and clear logs so problems can be found quickly.

Who it is for: Founders adding an AI feature to a product: The AI feature works in a demo but is slow or unpredictable in real use. A service with time limits, fallbacks and logs between the app and the model lets a slow or failing answer be traced to its cause. Startups building a first backend: A small team needs a documented API, a database and tests behind a website or mobile app. I keep the core logic as plain tested code, so the product is easier to extend later. Teams with a backend nobody dares to touch: Every change risks breaking something, and the original author may have moved on. I read the code, add tests around what must not change, fix the slow parts and make failures visible. Operations teams linking internal systems: Two tools hold related data, and people retype it or wait for slow jobs. I build the link as an API with background workers and live progress on a web screen, so nobody watches a frozen page.

Problems I solve: A slow or failing request cannot be explained. I add a request ID (a label that follows one request through the logs), metrics and traces. In my traceable AI backend, a trace exposed a deliberately slow lookup on made-up data, and indexing cut it from about 15 seconds to under 50 milliseconds. An AI step takes minutes for every request. I measure where the time goes. On a drafting service at work, I found hidden extra processing in how the AI models were called and compared four candidate models. Time per request fell from 7.9 minutes to 16.9 seconds, with accuracy unchanged. Slow jobs freeze the app for everyone. Heavy work goes to background workers (Celery and Redis), and progress is pushed to the screen over WebSockets. At an internship I set up both: workers so heavy jobs did not slow the main API, and live progress for long data-matching jobs. Wrong or missing input breaks the service. Every request is checked at the door, with Pydantic in FastAPI or serializers in Django REST Framework, and each wrong input gets a clear error message. The box-selection API I submitted for a job application has a test for each rejected case. Two systems hold the same data and drift apart. I build the sync as a documented API on PostgreSQL, check each record on the way in and log every run. At an internship I built backend APIs that sync data between internal company systems.

Deliverables: A backend API with documented endpoints, meaning the web addresses your app calls (FastAPI or Django REST Framework); A PostgreSQL database design, with scripts to update it safely; A Docker setup so the whole system starts the same way everywhere; Automated tests for the main logic and the API (pytest); Logs, speed metrics and request traces where they help; A README, API documentation and handover notes.

What I need from you: A list of the apps, screens or other systems that will call the API, and what each one needs back.; Access to the existing code, database layout and any notes, if a service already exists, so I can read it before changing anything.; Sample data that includes the messy cases, and a rough idea of how many users or requests to expect.; Where the system will run, who will look after it, and any rules on security, data location or monitoring..

Technology: FastAPI (Serves the API, checks every incoming request and writes interactive API documentation from the code.); Django and Django REST Framework (Suit products that also need an admin area and user accounts. The box-selection API I submitted uses them with an admin screen.); Pydantic (Describes the shape of each request and response, and rejects wrong input with a clear message.); PostgreSQL (Stores the application data. The table design and the scripts that update it safely are part of the handover.); Celery and Redis (Run slow work in background workers. Redis holds the queue of waiting jobs, so the main API stays quick.); WebSockets (Keep a live connection to the browser, so the progress of a long job appears on a React screen as it happens.); pytest (Runs automated tests on the core logic and on each endpoint, including the inputs that must be rejected.); Docker and Docker Compose (Package the system so it starts the same way on any machine. Compose starts the API and its helpers together.); OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Jaeger (Metrics count requests and timings, and traces show each step of one request, so slow calls can be explained.).

Trade-offs: FastAPI or Django. An API-first service, especially one with AI calls, fits FastAPI. A product that needs staff admin screens and user accounts fits Django. If your team already knows one of them, that often decides it, because someone has to maintain the code. Background queue or direct call. A job that finishes in a second or two can run inside the request. One that takes minutes needs a queue, background workers and a progress channel. A queue adds parts to run and watch, so I measure real job times first. How much monitoring to add. Full tracing, dashboards and alerts take time to build and to read. For a first version I add request IDs in the logs and tests on the core logic. Metrics and traces follow when traffic, cost or risk justify them.

Where it fits: Shipping and e-commerce teams: A service that takes an order and returns a recommendation, such as the fewest and cheapest shipping boxes, with strict input checks and tests that cover every rejected case. Audit and compliance teams: A service that connects an AI drafting or document-reading tool to an existing product, with bulk upload, review screens and checks that block invented data. Data and operations teams: A matching service that compares two large lists of records in stages, shows live progress while it runs and replaces slow compare-everything loops with sorted searches. Product teams with an AI feature: An API in front of language models (LLMs) with request limits, model fallbacks, logs and traces, so slow or failing answers can be explained and costs stay visible.

Q: Is FastAPI used in production? A: Yes. Many companies use FastAPI in production for web services and AI features. It is fast, checks incoming data automatically and writes API documentation for you. At work I built an AI drafting service in FastAPI that runs next to a live product. I use it for real systems, not only for demos.

Q: Which is better, FastAPI or Django? A: FastAPI suits services built around an API, including AI features. Django with Django REST Framework suits products that also need an admin area, user accounts and a built-in database layer. I use both and will recommend one after reading your requirements.

Q: Can you take over an existing Python backend? A: Yes. Much of my professional work has been inside existing systems. I read the code before changing it and keep changes covered by tests. I also leave a clear decision log in the repository, so your team knows what changed and why.

Q: Can you set up background jobs and live progress updates? A: Yes. I have used Celery and Redis to move slow work away from the main API. I have also used WebSockets to stream the progress of long-running jobs to a React web screen. Users see live status instead of waiting, and the main API stays responsive for everyone else.

Q: Will the API come with tests? A: Yes. My own backend projects ship with tests on the core logic and on each endpoint. The box-selection API, a job-application task, has 27 passing tests, and the traceable AI backend has 10 that run offline. I take the same approach on client work. Tests make later changes safer and show your team how each part should behave.

Q: How much does API development cost in India? A: Price depends on the number of endpoints, the systems the API must connect to, the state of your data, and how much testing and documentation you want. A clearly defined scope can be quoted at a fixed price. Open-ended work is usually fairer by the hour. I quote after reading a short brief, with terms agreed in writing.

Q: How do you keep a FastAPI backend secure? A: Every request is checked, and wrong input is rejected with a clear message. I add request limits, such as 1 per second with bursts of 5 on an AI chat service I co-built, and can add sign-in with per-key usage quotas. For sensitive data the AI model can run on your own servers. Plan a security review before launch.

Q: What API documentation will I receive? A: FastAPI builds interactive documentation from the code itself, so it stays in step with what the API does. Alongside it you receive a README with setup steps and example requests, and handover notes on how the parts fit. A web or mobile developer can start from the same written description.

# Computer vision development services
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/services/computer-vision/
Freelance computer vision developer in Mumbai. Tools that detect, count and classify things in photos and video with OpenCV, PyTorch and YOLOv8.

I offer computer vision development services: software that finds, counts or sorts things in photos and video. Examples are crowd counting, spotting events in camera footage and matching faces. I measure how accurate it is on your own footage and report what it was tested on. I also deliver a small app or report your team can use.

Who it is for: Facility and safety managers: People who must watch how busy a space gets. They need counts, an alert at a set limit and a saved frame as evidence. A team prototype I worked on counts people crossing a line in recorded video. Product teams adding video checks: Teams that want a first-pass screen for uploaded videos or images, such as flagging possible face-swap edits, with a clear report and an honest accuracy figure before they invest more. Security and operations leads: Teams with more cameras and photos than people to review them. A tool pre-sorts the material, so staff look at a short list of flagged items instead of everything. Research and student teams: Groups that need a documented, repeatable detection or classification workflow, with the data split and results written down so another person can rerun it and get the same numbers.

Problems I solve: Too much footage for people to review. Video analytics software samples frames, counts people or labels possible events, and saves the frame behind each result. A person then checks only the flagged moments. The team CCTV prototype works this way on recorded video. Accuracy figures that do not hold up. In project work I keep test footage apart from training footage, split by video, and state the split beside every figure. The team deepfake detector's 74.16% is labelled as a random frame-level split, because near-identical frames from one video can sit on both sides. Busy, dark or blurry scenes confuse the model. Simple background removal can undercount when people overlap. I test on your hardest footage and report where the tool fails. For crowded scenes I can switch to a trained detector with a tracker (it follows each person from frame to frame). Reviewers cannot see why something was flagged. Each result keeps the evidence behind it. In the deepfake app, a chart scores every frame, a note explains each confidence band and a PDF report can be downloaded. The CCTV prototype saves its evidence frames in MongoDB. Alerts do not reach the right person. Alerts go to a channel your staff already use. The CCTV prototype I worked on sent a WhatsApp message through Twilio when the crowd limit was reached, with a reference to the saved frame.

Deliverables: A detection or classification tool for your images or video; Code that samples video frames and cleans them up first (OpenCV); A short results note that states how the tool was tested; A small Streamlit or Flask app for uploading files and viewing results; Alerts or record-keeping, such as saving to a database or sending a WhatsApp message (Twilio); A documented repository or notebook, so results can be reproduced.

What I need from you: Sample footage or images from the real setting, with permission to use them, covering the angles, lighting and times of day that matter.; A clear list of what must be detected or counted, and which mistake costs you more: a missed event or a false alarm.; Someone who knows your site and can mark the correct answers on a sample of footage, because accuracy is measured against those marks.; The setup: how many cameras, recorded clips or a live stream, the hardware available, and where alerts should be sent..

Technology: OpenCV (Reads video, samples frames, resizes and cleans images, and handles background removal, line-crossing counts and classic face matching.); YOLOv8 (A fast detector that draws a box around each object. I have run the small YOLOv8n model on video frames.); PyTorch (Runs ready-made detection and classification models, including Faster R-CNN and the Vision Transformer used for crime labels.); TensorFlow / Keras (Trains small image networks on labelled frames, as in the college deepfake detector, and saves them for an app to load.); Hugging Face Transformers (Loads a ready-made Vision Transformer for frame labels, so a first baseline needs no training.); Streamlit (Builds the upload-and-review app, with a confidence chart and a downloadable PDF report made with ReportLab.); Flask (Serves simple pages where reviewers see the latest detections and saved evidence frames.); MongoDB (Stores evidence frames and crime labels, so alerts can be checked later.); Twilio (Sends WhatsApp alerts, such as a message when a crowd limit is crossed.).

Trade-offs: Ready-made model or custom training. A ready-made detector is quick and often good enough for common objects such as people. Custom training pays off for unusual objects or camera views. I test a ready-made model on your footage first and train only if the numbers fall short. Fewer false alarms or fewer misses. A detector can be tuned to raise fewer false alarms or to miss fewer real events, but not both at once. We agree which mistake costs more for you, set the alert level to match and report both kinds of error. Every frame or a frame every few seconds. Checking one frame every few seconds is light on hardware and often enough to label events or count who is in view. Counting people as they cross a line needs every frame. The team CCTV prototype used both. I measure speed on your hardware before we choose.

Where it fits: Car parks and logistics yards: Count vehicles at a gate camera, log the totals by hour and show staff how full the site is. Shops and service counters: Estimate how many people are waiting and tell staff when a queue passes a set length, so they open another counter in time. Media and platform safety teams: Run a first-pass screen on uploaded videos for possible face-swap edits and hand a reviewer a frame-by-frame report with confidence scores, with a person making the final call. Recycling and waste handling: Sort photos of items into categories, so people check only the doubtful cases, as in my internship classifier for plastic-waste images.

Q: What is YOLO object detection? A: YOLO, short for You Only Look Once, is a fast method that finds and labels objects in an image or video frame. It works in one pass and draws a box around each. I have used the small YOLOv8n version on video frames. It suits live counting and alerts, though accuracy has to be tested on your own footage.

Q: How accurate is computer vision? A: Accuracy is measured on a sample of your own footage first, using data the model has not seen. The result is reported clearly, together with the way the data was split. The deepfake detector from my college team reports 74.16% on a random frame-level split, so every figure states what it covers.

Q: How much does a computer vision project cost? A: It depends on how much footage or how many images you have, how much labelling is needed, the accuracy you need and whether the tool must run live. I do not publish a price list. After a short brief I suggest a fixed price or hourly billing for a clear scope, and we agree it in writing before I start.

Q: Can you train a model on my own images or video? A: Yes, for small to medium sets of images. A college team I was part of trained a neural network on frames from a public deepfake dataset, and during an internship I built one that sorts plastic-waste images. I have also used ready-made models such as Faster R-CNN, YOLOv8n and a Vision Transformer. We first check your labelled data.

Q: Can it work on live camera feeds? A: The team CCTV prototype read recorded video and checked frames on a schedule, one every three seconds for the crime labels. Live feeds are a different job: real-time speed depends on camera quality, the number of cameras and your hardware. I would connect a test stream and measure that during planning rather than assume it.

Q: What about privacy for face or surveillance projects? A: Those projects need consent, clear rules on how long data is kept and legal review on your side. I raise privacy questions during planning and can build in options such as limited data retention and restricted access to stored images. The legal decisions stay with you.

Q: Can computer vision count people in a crowd? A: Yes, within limits. The CCTV prototype I worked on counted people crossing virtual lines using OpenCV background removal and raised an alert at a set limit. Dense or dark scenes are harder, so I would test on your own footage and, if needed, move to a trained detector and tracker for steadier counts.

Q: Does my video have to be uploaded to an online service? A: Not necessarily. Detection models such as YOLOv8 run on your own computer or server, so video can stay in your building. In the CCTV prototype I worked on, the README calls for a local MongoDB database for evidence frames, and the WhatsApp alert carried only a short text. The right setup depends on your privacy rules and hardware.

# Machine learning model development for speech, text and data
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/services/speech-nlp-ml/
Freelance machine learning developer in Mumbai. Models that learn from audio, text or spreadsheet data, with accuracy tested on your data and a web app.

I offer machine learning model development: models that learn from sound, text or spreadsheet data. Examples are detecting emotion in a voice clip, filtering spam messages and predicting prices. Each model comes with accuracy measured on your own data and a note on how it was tested. A small web app lets non-technical people try it themselves.

Who it is for: Teams with voice recordings: Teams that want to flag tone or mood in recorded calls or check-ins, such as calls worth a follow-up, and need to know how far the labels can be trusted. Support and messaging teams: Teams that receive many emails or texts and want unwanted messages filtered out automatically, with very few genuine messages blocked by mistake. Analysts with spreadsheet data: People who hold tables of past results and want to predict a number, such as a price or a cost, and see how much a stronger model adds over a simple one. Founders testing an idea: Product owners who need a quick proof of concept on their own labelled data, with a clear accuracy figure, before they fund a bigger build.

Problems I solve: A model's accuracy figure cannot be trusted. In project work I hold back a test set the model never sees, split by speaker or source where possible, and state the split. I report precision (how many flags were right) and recall (how many real cases were found), not accuracy alone. It is unclear whether a complex model is needed. I train a simple baseline first, then the stronger model, and report both. In my house-price model a Random Forest (many decision trees averaged) reached an R-squared of 0.89 (1.0 is perfect) against 0.80 for a simple linear baseline, both on held-out houses. Raw audio and text are not ready for a model. Audio becomes numbers for loudness (energy), how often the signal crosses zero and MFCCs (a compact description of a voice's sound), extracted with librosa. Text is cleaned and scored by word frequency (TF-IDF). Tables get gaps filled and values scaled. Too few labelled examples. Before any training I count examples per category and report gaps early. Where audio is scarce, altering clips with noise and pitch changes adds variety: in the speech model I retrained, 12,162 clips became 48,648 samples. A trained model sits unused in a notebook. I wrap it in a small Streamlit app where people upload, record or paste and see the result, and in a tested FastAPI service when your own software must call it.

Deliverables: Data preparation and feature extraction (librosa for audio, word-frequency scoring for text, pandas for tables); Model training, with a comparison against a simple baseline; A results report that states how the data was split; A Streamlit app: upload, record or paste, then see the result; A saved model and a script that uses it; A reproducible notebook and a README.

What I need from you: Labelled examples: recordings, messages or table rows, each marked with the correct answer by someone who knows the subject.; A plain statement of what the model should predict, which mistakes cost most and what accuracy would make it useful.; Details of how the data was collected: speakers, devices, sources and dates, and any person or customer who appears many times.; Whether the data holds personal information, where it may be stored, and where the finished model must run..

Technology: librosa (Loads audio and measures it, giving the model numbers for loudness, zero-crossing rate and MFCCs.); TensorFlow / Keras (Trains neural networks, such as the five-block network I retrained for speech emotion, and saves them for reuse.); scikit-learn (Provides TF-IDF word scoring, Naive Bayes, Random Forest and linear models, plus data splits and accuracy measures.); NLTK (Handles natural language processing (NLP) steps: splits text into words, drops common words and reduces each word to its stem.); pandas (Loads and cleans tables and datasets, and fills gaps such as missing values with the median.); Streamlit (Builds the small app where people upload, record or paste, then see the result with a chart.); sounddevice (Records short microphone clips, so a model can be tried live on a voice.); Hugging Face Transformers (Loads ready-made pretrained models to use as a first baseline before any training from scratch.); FastAPI (Serves a saved model as an API that your own software can call, with tests and a Docker setup.).

Trade-offs: Simple baseline or neural network. A simple model such as Naive Bayes or a linear fit is quick to build and easy to explain. A neural network may add accuracy on audio or images. I build the simple one first and keep the stronger model only if the gap justifies the extra complexity. Test on new speakers or random samples. A random split is quick, but it can flatter the result when one speaker or source appears on both sides. Splitting by speaker, customer or source gives a lower, fairer number. On your data I split that way where possible; my speech project used a random split. Fewer wrong blocks or fewer misses. A filter can be tuned to avoid blocking genuine messages or to catch more spam, but not both at once. On its 1,034 test messages my spam filter flagged no genuine message and missed 30 spam messages. We choose by what each mistake costs you.

Where it fits: Customer support centres: Flag recorded calls where the caller sounds angry or upset, so supervisors listen to those first. Accuracy would be tested on your own recordings before any use. Wellbeing and coaching apps: Show the mood heard in a short voice check-in as a probability for each emotion, not one hard label, and never as a medical result. Telecom and messaging platforms: Filter unwanted texts with a light word-frequency model that can be tuned so genuine messages are rarely blocked, then retrained on new examples. Finance and property analysts: Estimate a price or cost from a few facts about each case, compare a simple baseline with a stronger model, and see the typical error in plain units.

Q: How do you deploy a machine learning model? A: A trained model is wrapped in a small FastAPI service with tests and a Docker setup, the same way I build other backends. Your apps can then send data to it and read the result. Handover includes instructions for running it, so your team can move it to a server or cloud machine later.

Q: How much data do I need to train a model? A: It depends on the task. Simple tasks with clear categories may need a few hundred labelled examples per category, while audio or images usually need thousands. My spam filter used 5,169 messages after duplicates were removed, and my speech model 12,162 clips. I count your examples first and tell you early if there are too few.

Q: Can you classify my own audio or text data? A: Yes, if you have labelled examples and a clear target. I have built a neural network on audio features. I have also built a spam classifier on text (word-frequency scoring with a Naive Bayes classifier). Each has a small app around it. Before training, we check that you have enough examples of each category.

Q: How do you report accuracy? A: Every figure comes with the data split it was measured on. The speech emotion model I retrained reaches 93.87% on a random 20% test split. Because that split can put altered copies of one clip on both sides, it says little about new voices. For your recordings I test on speakers the model has not heard.

Q: Do you use ready-made models? A: When they fit. Pretrained Hugging Face models are a sensible start for many text and audio tasks. My speech model began as a public training recipe that I retrained and tested on four datasets. I compare against a simple baseline, so you see what extra complexity buys, and I say when the simple option is enough.

Q: Can you build a prediction model from my spreadsheet data? A: Yes, if you have past rows with the outcome you want to predict, such as a price or cost. I clean the table, fill gaps, compare a simple linear baseline with a stronger model such as a Random Forest, and report the typical error in your own units. A small app lets your team try it.

Q: How do you check a model has not just memorised its data? A: I keep a test set the model never trains on and compare its score there with its training score. A large gap means it has memorised. The speech network I retrained also uses dropout (switching off random parts during training) to limit this. For your audio, altered copies of a clip stay on one side of the split.

Q: Can you check the accuracy of a model someone else built? A: Yes. I need the saved model or code, the data it used and the figure that was claimed. I rerun it, check how the data was split, compare it with a simple baseline and report what I measure. The same habit exposed a flattering 93% score on a bank text-to-SQL assistant, where running the queries showed far less.

Who it is for: Small businesses answering the same questions daily: Staff spend hours on the same questions. Trade-offs: Polling or a webhook. Polling (the bot keeps asking for new messages) is the simplest way to run a small bot, even from a laptop, but works only while the program runs. # Healthcare RAG chatbot that cites its sources
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/ai-rag-healthcare-assistant/
Case study: a chatbot using FastAPI, ChromaDB and Groq that answers from six made-up health policies, cites its source and refuses off-topic questions.

This healthcare RAG chatbot answers questions from six made-up healthcare policy documents. RAG means it looks up the right passages first and then writes the answer from them. It returns its source and a confidence label, and refuses out-of-scope questions instead of guessing.

Clinics, hospital groups, insurers and health-software teams keep their rules in long documents: appointment rules, refill limits, discharge instructions, privacy policy and billing terms. Staff and patients ask the same questions again and again. A chatbot can answer them, but in healthcare it is only useful if people can trust what it says and check where it came from.

A good result answers only from your own documents and shows the document and passage behind each answer. When the documents are silent, it says "not found" and points the person to the facility instead of guessing. Booking requests go to a scheduling tool (a mock in this prototype), and the prompts are plain text that a non-programmer can review. This project shows that behaviour on made-up policies.

Problem: Healthcare answers must come from the right document. A confident wrong answer is worse than no answer. Policies are long, staff and patients ask about them again and again, and a wrong answer can mean a missed rule, a complaint or a compliance problem. An answer with no source also cannot be checked, so a reviewer cannot trust it.

What made it hard: Wrong answers cost more. In a healthcare setting a confident wrong answer is worse than no answer, so the chatbot must show its source and be able to refuse. Telling questions apart. Booking requests, small talk and policy questions need different handling. A question such as "how are telehealth visits billed?" starts like small talk but is a policy question. Keeping the AI inside the documents. A language model uses what it already knows unless told not to. The prompt had to forbid outside knowledge and medical advice, and weak matches had to be stopped before the model saw them. Hosted models get retired. The settings file records two of the models I used as deprecated by the provider. The service needs a backup list that can change without code edits.

Approach: I built the chatbot as a small FastAPI service with three safety layers. First, a router works out what the user wants: a booking request, small talk or a policy question. Second, for policy questions the six documents are searched by meaning, and weak matches are dropped before the AI is called. Third, a strict instruction forces an exact fallback sentence when nothing relevant remains. Each answer drawn from the documents returns its source, a short excerpt and a confidence label. Settings and prompts live in plain files, and a chain of backup AI models keeps the service running if one is retired.

My part: All the application code: the FastAPI service, document loading and search, the router, the prompts and the Streamlit chat screen. Sole author, 28 commits. The safety design: the score threshold, the exact fallback sentence, the strict prompts and the confidence label on every reply. The settings and operations side: settings files, the backup model chain, request IDs in the logs and the Docker packaging. The 6 quick automated tests, a written list of sample questions with expected answers and a script that calls the running server. Fixes made along the way: repeat loading no longer creates duplicate chunks, the chat screen escapes text and a double-send bug is gone.

Context: It was a take-home prototype. The six policy documents are made up and the scheduling tool is a mock, so nothing connects to a real clinic system or real patient data. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a standard public pattern. ChromaDB, sentence-transformers and the hosted Groq model are existing tools that I configured and connected, not things I trained. There is no live demo. The code is public, and the service runs locally or in Docker.

Architecture: Six made-up policy documents (appointments, discharge, health-privacy rules, insurance, refills and telehealth) are read from plain text files and cut into chunks of 500 characters with an overlap of 50; Meaning-based search: sentence-transformers turns each chunk into numbers, stored in ChromaDB on disk. The model runs on the CPU and is baked into the Docker image, and the top 3 matches are used; A three-way router based on keywords: booking requests go to a mock scheduling tool, small talk to a friendly persona and everything else to the document chatbot; A similarity score threshold, set in the settings, drops weak matches before the AI is called. If nothing passes, a fixed "not found" reply is returned and the AI is not called at all; A strict instruction with an exact fallback sentence. Each answer drawn from the documents returns the source document, a short excerpt of the passage and a confidence label based on how many documents matched; A chain of backup Groq models: if one fails or is retired, the next is tried and the reply names the model that answered. Prompts and settings live in plain files; A FastAPI backend with health, ingest and ask endpoints, input limits and a request ID on the log lines of each request, a Streamlit chat screen and Docker packaging.

Design decisions: Drop weak matches before the AI. I filter retrieved passages by a similarity score and return a fixed "not found" reply, without calling the AI, when none pass. The AI cannot misuse a passage it never sees, and an out-of-scope question costs no AI call. The threshold is a setting, so it can be made stricter without touching code. Send unclear questions to the documents. I used plain keyword rules to separate booking, small talk and policy questions. Anything unclear goes to document search, not to the chat persona. Rules are easy to read and test. A misrouted policy question still meets the score threshold and the strict prompt, which is safer than a friendly reply that invents facts. Keep prompts and settings in files. Prompt wording sits in plain text files, and the main tunable values (models, threshold, chunk size, input limits, which websites may call the API) sit in settings, not in the code. A reviewer who does not write code can read the prompt, changes show up as plain text differences, and tuning or swapping a model does not mean editing the code. A chain of backup models. I made the model list a setting. The service tries the main Groq model, then each backup in order, and every reply from the model names the model that answered. Hosted models get retired. The settings file itself records two of the models I used as deprecated, and a backup list lets the service keep answering while I update it.

First attempt: My first version passed the top 3 passages to the AI whatever their score and relied on the prompt alone to refuse. Later I limited document search to questions containing a listed healthcare word, so anything else fell through to a canned greeting. What changed: I added a score threshold so weak matches never reach the AI, and made document search the default again for anything that is not a booking request or small talk. I then replaced the canned greetings with a persona prompt that may not invent facility facts.

Results: Each answer drawn from the documents returns its source document, a short excerpt of the passage used and a confidence label; Out-of-scope questions are meant to get a fixed fallback sentence, not a guess: weak matches never reach the AI, and the strict prompt asks it to use the same sentence when the passages do not answer; The service keeps running when a hosted model is retired, without a code change, because the backup models are a setting; 6 quick automated smoke tests check the health endpoint, input validation and document loading, and the backend is packaged in Docker; Each request gets a short ID that appears in its log lines and in the X-Request-ID response header, so one question can be followed through the logs; Re-loading unchanged documents does not create duplicate chunks, because each chunk gets a fixed ID built from its file name and text.

Limits: It reads only plain text files, runs on six made-up documents and has not been tried on real policy sets. It does not reload documents when a file changes, and old chunks stay until the collection is reset. The repository keeps no scored check of answer quality. The 12 sample questions (plus 2 out-of-scope ones) are a manual list with expected answers, and the confidence label comes from how many documents matched. It is not a probability. Routing uses keyword rules that can misread unusual wording. The booking tool is a mock, and there is no sign-in, no memory between questions and only a single language. Questions and the few passages used are sent to a hosted AI service. A real deployment would need your own documents, a privacy and legal review, secured hosting and probably a private model.

Where this fits: Clinics and hospital groups: Front-desk staff and patients ask about refills, discharge limits, privacy and billing. A cited assistant answers from the facility's own policies and sends booking requests onward. Insurers and claims teams: Policy holders ask what a plan covers or how to dispute a bill. The assistant answers from the plan documents and shows the passage behind each answer. HR and internal policy desks: Staff ask about leave, expenses or conduct rules. An assistant that cites the handbook and admits when the handbook is silent is meant to cut down repeat questions to HR. Banks and regulated firms: Staff must follow internal procedures and regulatory manuals. An assistant that answers with a source passage, or says "not found", lets a reviewer check every answer.

Role: Sole author. I wrote all of it (28 commits).

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Reading real document sets; Agents that use your tools; Better search and reranking; Scored question set and stricter checks; Speed and usage dashboards.

Q: How do you build a RAG chatbot? A: Cut your documents into chunks, turn each chunk into numbers a search index can compare, and store them. When a question arrives, find the best matching chunks, then ask an AI model to answer only from them. Here that used chunks of 500 with an overlap of 50, ChromaDB and the top 3 matches.

Q: How do you evaluate a RAG chatbot? A: Check three things. Does each answer cite the right source? Do out-of-scope questions get a plain "not found"? Are weak matches dropped before the AI is called? This prototype has 6 quick automated tests and a manual list of sample questions, but no scored check of answer quality. I would add that first for any real use.

Q: What happens when the answer is not in the documents? A: The chatbot says so. Weak matches are dropped before the AI is called, and the AI is told to use an exact fallback sentence when nothing relevant remains. That is how an out-of-scope question is meant to get a plain "not found" reply, pointing the person to the facility, instead of a confident guess.

Q: Does it use real patient data? A: No. It is a prototype built on six made-up policy documents and uses no real patient data. A real deployment would need the organisation's own documents, encrypted and access-controlled hosting, a privacy and legal review, agreements with any cloud provider that sees the data, and proper testing with the staff who will use it.

Q: Can this chatbot book real appointments? A: No. The scheduling tool is a mock. It picks a department and a day out of the question and returns four example time slots, marked as illustrative, with a note to call or use the patient portal to confirm. Real booking would mean connecting it to a real scheduling system, which I could build.

Q: Does the chatbot remember earlier questions in a chat? A: No. The chat screen shows the conversation so far, but the backend answers each question on its own, so a follow-up such as "and what about children?" carries no context. Adding memory is the improvement I listed for this project, and it needs care so old answers do not mix with new passages.

Q: What does the chatbot send to the hosted AI service? A: At question time, only the last step goes online. The model that searches the documents runs on the server's own processor. For each question, the question text and the few matching passages are sent to the hosted Groq model, which writes the answer. For private data, a model on the organisation's own servers would be used.

---

# CCTV video analytics in Python: crowds, crime and faces
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/advanced-cctv-analytics/
Case study: a Smart India Hackathon team project that watches one CCTV video three ways: crowd-limit alerts, crime labels and face recognition.

CCTV video analytics in Python: this Smart India Hackathon team prototype watches camera footage three ways. A crowd counter raises a limit alert, a crime module labels sampled video frames and a face module recognises enrolled people. The crowd and crime modules save evidence frames to MongoDB and send WhatsApp alerts. Co-built with Prasanna Patil.

Shops, event venues, campuses and transport hubs often run more cameras than their security staff can watch at once. Crowds build past a safe size, fights start and people who should not be on site walk in, often while a screen goes unwatched. Software that watches the footage, sends a short alert and keeps the picture behind it is meant to help a small team spot these moments sooner.

A good result is an alert that a person can trust and check. It says what was seen, keeps the frame behind it and does not flood the team with false alarms. For a buyer, that means measuring each alert type on their own footage before relying on it, and setting privacy rules before any face data is stored.

Problem: Public-safety teams cannot watch every camera at once. Overcrowding, violent incidents and known persons of interest slip past exactly when attention matters most. The cost is a slower response, more risk to the people on site and more damage or liability for the venue, because a team that checks screens by eye can only react after someone happens to notice.

What made it hard: Overlapping people in a crowd. People who walk close together merge into one moving shape. The sample crowd clip in the repository is a dense street scene, so counting by shapes is rough and every count is an estimate. Judging crime from a still frame. The classifier sees one picture every 3 seconds, with no sense of movement, so the context that makes an event a crime is often missing. Its labels are hints for a person to check. Alerts that come with evidence. A bare alarm is hard to trust or act on. Each alert needs a saved frame and, for crime, a label to check. That means storing images and reading them back for review. Faces are personal data. Recognising a person means keeping their face photos. That raises consent, retention and access questions that this prototype does not yet handle.

Approach: The prototype splits monitoring into three separate modules. The crowd module removes the video background to find moving shapes, tracks each shape and counts people crossing two virtual lines, then raises an alert at a set limit. The crime module checks one frame every 3 seconds with a pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT, an image-classification model) that returns one of 14 labels. The face module finds faces with Haar cascades (a classic face finder) and names them with an LBPH matcher (a classic face-matching method), after a small tool enrols the people to look for. The crowd and crime modules save evidence frames to MongoDB and send alerts through Twilio WhatsApp. Flask pages show the latest saved frame.

My part: Worked as a member of the Smart India Hackathon team and co-built the prototype with Prasanna Patil. Shared in the team's win of the college's internal round of the Smart India Hackathon. Kept a copy of the team's repository on my account. It was first uploaded from my co-builder's account, my only commit is a README line, and I claim no sole credit.

Context: The code was uploaded in one batch, so its history cannot show who wrote which module. I describe all three modules as shared team work. The crime classifier is a published model loaded by name from the Hugging Face model hub. The repository holds no training code for it. The crowd counter's tracker and line counting follow a public people-counter example, and the face tool follows public OpenCV tutorials. Some crowd page buttons and lights are placeholders.

Architecture: Crowd module: OpenCV background subtraction (MOG2) finds moving shapes, and a simple tracker gives each one an ID. Two virtual lines count people crossing in each direction. At the limit of 12 it saves the frame, beeps twice, sends a WhatsApp alert and starts the review page server.; Crime module: a pre-trained Vision Transformer, published on the Hugging Face model hub as UCF_Crime, labels one frame every 3 seconds with one of 14 UCF-Crime labels: 13 incident types, such as Fighting or Robbery, and a normal label.; Face module: Haar cascades locate faces in a webcam image. A small tkinter window enrols a person by saving cropped 200 by 200 pixel photos, and an LBPH matcher then shows a name, or "not recognized", on screen.; Evidence store: the crowd and crime modules save each evidence frame as an image in MongoDB, a database. The crime module keeps the label with the frame and skips a frame whose exact pixels were already stored.; Review pages: two small Flask pages show the latest saved frame from MongoDB, one for crowd alerts and one for crime labels, where the label sits above the picture.; Alerts: the Twilio WhatsApp API sends a short text when the crowd limit is reached, carrying the ID of the saved frame, and one text when the crime module finishes a video. Neither message includes the picture.; Inputs and settings: the crowd and crime modules read a video file chosen in a file dialog, and the face tool reads a webcam. The crowd limit and the crime sampling interval are plain variables in the scripts..

Design decisions: Three separate modules, not one pipeline. Crowd counting, crime labelling and face recognition are separate programs, each with its own input and settings. The crowd and crime programs each have their own review page. Each can be run, tested and replaced on its own, and a fault in one does not stop the others. The cost is that they do not yet share one feed or one dashboard. A published crime model, not a new one. The crime module loads a Vision Transformer published on the Hugging Face model hub as UCF_Crime, with the 14 UCF-Crime labels. The repository holds no training code. It gives usable labels without collecting and labelling footage first. The trade-off is that its accuracy on a buyer's own cameras is unknown until it is measured. Classic OpenCV methods for people and faces. The prototype finds people by background subtraction and counting lines, from a public example, and faces by Haar cascades with an LBPH matcher, rather than a trained detector. These methods are light, need no training data for counting and only a few dozen photos per person for faces. The trade-off is weaker results in dense crowds, poor light and side-on faces. Evidence frames stored in MongoDB. Each alert keeps its frame as an image in MongoDB, and a Flask page reads back the latest one for a reviewer. A reviewer sees what the system saw, not only a text alert. The trade-off is growing storage and the need for access and retention rules for stored images.

Results: Three separate monitoring modules: a crowd counter, a crime labeller and a face recogniser.; The crime model has 14 labels, 13 incident types and a normal label, and the code checks one frame every 3 seconds. Both are settings read from the code, not measured accuracy.; On the sample crowd clip in the repository, the counter reached its limit of 12 crossings. The saved frame and a count log with 12 entries are kept with the code.; The crowd and crime modules save evidence frames and labels to MongoDB, with Flask pages that show the latest saved frame.; The team won the college's internal round of the Smart India Hackathon..

Limits: No accuracy was measured. Counts, crime labels and face matches were not tested against labelled footage, so the prototype shows the idea and the working parts, not a reliability figure. The crowd limit counts people crossing downward, not people present at once. Line positions are fixed numbers, overlapping shapes are likely to be counted as one, and the program stops after its first alert. The crime module takes the top label for each sampled frame, with no confidence cut-off, on a 3-second timer that follows the computer clock, not the video. Its one WhatsApp text goes out when the video ends, whatever was found. It is a set of desktop scripts for one computer, reading video files or a local webcam, not network camera streams, with no automated tests. Keys, phone numbers and paths sit inside the code, and the keys are blank in the public copy.

Where this fits: Shopping centres and event venues: Count people at an entrance and alert staff when a safe limit is reached, with a saved frame for the record. Retail stores: Flag possible shoplifting or fights for a person to review, without staff watching every screen all day. Each flag keeps its frame. Campuses and housing societies: Watch gates and corridors after hours and message a guard when a crowd builds, with a saved frame, and show staff when an enrolled person is matched. Security service providers: Give monitoring staff a first-pass filter across many sites, so people look at flagged moments first, once each alert type is measured on site footage.

Role: Member of the Smart India Hackathon team. Co-built with Prasanna Patil.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Modern people detector and tracker; Live camera stream input; Accuracy testing on your footage; Alert dashboard and rules; Privacy controls.

Q: What is video analytics in CCTV? A: Video analytics is software that watches camera footage and reports what it sees, such as how many people are in a place, unusual events or known faces. This prototype has three separate modules: crowd counting with an alert, crime labels from sampled frames and face recognition. The crowd and crime modules save their evidence to a database.

Q: How accurate is the crime classifier? A: I do not quote an accuracy figure, because I did not measure one on labelled footage. The module uses a pre-trained Vision Transformer with 14 UCF-Crime labels and checks one frame every 3 seconds. A real project would start by measuring it on footage from your own site, then tune the alert rules.

Q: Did you build all of it yourself? A: No. It was a team project, co-built with Prasanna Patil for the Smart India Hackathon. I was a member of the team and I do not claim sole credit for any module. The code was uploaded in one batch from his account, so its history cannot show who wrote what. The team won the college's internal round.

Q: How does the crowd counter decide when to raise an alert? A: It removes the video background to find moving shapes, tracks each one and counts people who cross a virtual line. When the count reaches the limit, set to 12 in the code, it saves the frame to MongoDB, beeps, sends a WhatsApp text and stops. The limit counts crossings downward, not people present at once.

Q: How does the face recognition part work? A: A small window enrols a person by saving cropped photos from a webcam. OpenCV's LBPH recogniser, a classic face-matching method, is then trained on those photos. Haar cascades find faces in the live image and the screen shows a name or "not recognized". It follows public tutorials, sends no alerts and keeps no evidence frames, only the enrolment photos.

Q: Which crimes can the model label? A: The model has 14 labels: Abuse, Arrest, Arson, Assault, Burglary, Explosion, Fighting, Road accidents, Robbery, Shooting, Shoplifting, Stealing, Vandalism and a normal-video label. It picks one label for each sampled frame, with no confidence cut-off, so a label is a hint for a person to check and not a finding.

Q: Is this prototype ready for a real control room? A: No. It is a hackathon prototype made of desktop scripts that run on one computer and read video files or a webcam. Settings sit inside the code and there are no automated tests. A real deployment would need network camera input, accuracy tests on your footage, alert rules, privacy controls and monitoring.
