# Speech emotion recognition project
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/speech-emotion-recognition/
Case study: a neural network that labels seven emotions in speech, trained on four public datasets. 93.87% on a random test split, with a live mic demo.

This speech emotion recognition project is a neural network (a 1-D CNN, which reads audio as a sequence) that labels seven emotions in speech clips. It was trained on four public datasets and scored 93.87% on a random 20% test split. It comes with live microphone input and a web dashboard.

Teams that record customer calls or voice messages cannot listen to every recording. Mood can show in the voice as well as in the words, so a caller who sounds angry or frightened can be missed by a search of the transcript. A model that labels emotion from audio could help a team decide which recordings deserve a person's time.

A good result is a model that labels the emotion in a short clip, shows how sure it is, and comes with a score that says how it was measured and what it does not prove. This project is that first step, on public recordings of speakers. Using it on real calls would need a fresh test on that team's own audio.

Problem: Emotion lives in tone, pitch and energy, not in the words, so a text-based model is the wrong tool. A transcript of a call keeps the words and loses the tone, so an angry caller and a calm one can read the same. A team that works from text alone can miss the very signal that shows which customers need a person.

What made it hard: Four datasets, one label set. The four public datasets cover emotions differently: CREMA-D has no surprise clips and RAVDESS has a separate calm label. They had to be merged into one set of seven labels, with calm counted as neutral. Uneven emotion examples. Surprise has 652 clips, against 1,923 for each of angry, disgust, fear, happy and sad. The model sees far fewer examples of it, and the test set holds only 505 surprise samples. Long training time. The network has 7.19 million parameters. Its 20 training passes took about ten hours in total, roughly half an hour each, so every retrain is a planned run, not a quick test. A score that can flatter. Altered copies of one clip can sit on both sides of the split, the same speakers appear on both sides, and the test split doubled as the validation set. The score can therefore overstate how well it handles new voices.

Approach: I started from a public training recipe on Kaggle and adapted it. The four datasets are merged into 12,162 labelled clips, and each clip becomes four versions: the original plus three altered copies, giving 48,648 examples. librosa turns each example into 2,376 numbers that describe the sound of the voice. A five-block neural network then learns seven emotions from those numbers. I tested it on a random 20% of the examples and serve it through notebooks, including live microphone input, and a Streamlit dashboard.

My part: Adapting the public Kaggle training recipe and retraining the network on the four merged datasets. Testing the retrained model on a random 20% split, reading the per-emotion scores and stating the limits of that test plainly. The inference notebook: it loads the saved model, predicts from an audio file and listens to the microphone in a live loop. The Streamlit dashboard: upload or record audio, then see the emotion, its confidence and a probability bar for every class, plus waveform and spectrogram views. Saving the model design, scaler and label encoder as files and publishing the notebooks in a public repository.

Context: The training recipe (data merge, audio altering, features and the 1-D network) comes from a public Kaggle notebook. I adapted and retrained it. The model design is not my own invention. The four datasets are public collections of speakers reading fixed sentences or words in each emotion. I recorded no audio, and no real calls or customers were involved. The dashboard is a local prototype. The public repository holds the notebooks, the model design and the preprocessing files, not the dashboard or the large trained weights.

Architecture: Four public datasets (RAVDESS, CREMA-D, TESS and SAVEE) merged into 12,162 clips, with RAVDESS calm recordings counted as neutral, so every clip has one of seven emotion labels.; Each clip is read as a 2.5-second window and made into four versions: the original, one with added noise, one pitch-shifted and one pitch-shifted with noise. That gives 48,648 samples.; librosa audio features: zero-crossing rate, energy and MFCCs (numbers that describe the sound of a voice), 2,376 numbers per sample, put on one scale with a scaler fitted on the training data only.; A five-block 1-D neural network (convolution, normalisation and pooling) with steps to prevent overfitting (memorising the training clips), then a 512-unit layer and a seven-way output. It has 7.19 million parameters.; Training uses the Adam optimiser for 20 passes over a random 80% of the samples (38,918), in batches of 64. The other 20% (9,730) is the test set.; A notebook for live microphone input: it records 2.5 seconds at a time, extracts the same features, scales them and prints the predicted emotion, then repeats until stopped.; A Streamlit dashboard: upload a WAV file or record, then see the emotion, its confidence, class probabilities and waveform and spectrogram views..

Design decisions: Adapt a public recipe. I chose to adapt a public Kaggle training recipe over designing a network from scratch. The recipe already covered the data merge, audio altering and feature steps. My effort went into retraining it, testing it honestly and making it usable live from a microphone. Merge four datasets. I trained on four merged datasets (RAVDESS, CREMA-D, TESS and SAVEE) rather than on one. Together they hold 12,162 clips from 121 speakers, by the datasets' own descriptions. One dataset alone can have as few as two speakers and one recording style. Keep four versions of each clip. I kept the recipe's four versions of each clip (original, noise, pitch shift, pitch shift with noise) rather than training on the original clips alone. More varied examples make it harder for the network to lean on one recording's quirks. The cost is that copies of one clip can fall on both sides of the split, so the score does not prove new-voice accuracy. Report the final model. I report the score of the final saved model (93.87%) rather than the best single training pass (95.24%). Both numbers come from the same test split, and choosing the best pass by its test score would flatter the model. The final model is the one that is saved and used.

Results: Seven emotions are recognised: angry, disgust, fear, happy, neutral, sad and surprise.; 93.87% accuracy and a weighted F1 score of 0.94 (one number that balances missed cases against false alarms) on a random 20% test split of 9,730 samples.; Per-emotion F1 scores run from 0.92 (sad) to 0.97 (surprise), measured on the same test split.; The score is for the final model, the one that is saved and used. An earlier training pass reached 95.24% on the same split; I quote the final figure because picking the best pass would flatter the model.; Caution: the test split can hold altered copies of clips that were also used in training, so the score does not show how it performs on new speakers.; Live microphone detection runs in a notebook and in the Streamlit dashboard. It has not been scored, so no accuracy figure is claimed for live speech..

Limits: The test is not fully independent. Altered copies of one clip, and the same speakers, appear on both sides of the split, and the test split doubled as the validation set during training. Accuracy on new voices is likely to be lower. Every clip is a speaker reading fixed words or sentences in a requested emotion. Real calls bring background noise, phone-quality audio, other languages and mixed feelings, none of which this model has been tested on. It reads a 2.5-second window and picks one of seven labels. Longer speech, changing emotion and labels outside the seven are not handled, and live microphone use has not been scored. The dashboard is a local prototype, and the large trained weights are not in the public repository, so a real build would start from a fresh, tested package with its own accuracy check.

Where this fits: Call-quality and support teams: Teams that record customer calls could use emotion labels to choose which calls a person should listen to first, once the model has been tested on their own recordings. Wellbeing and coaching app makers: An app that asks people to speak could show a mood signal for a person to review, never as a diagnosis, after a careful test on its own users' voices. Voice assistant and phone menu teams: A voice assistant or phone menu could hand a caller who sounds upset to a person sooner, if the model is tested on that product's microphones and callers. Research and student teams: Anyone studying speech can use the same pipeline as a baseline: merge public datasets, extract features, train a network and report scores with their caveats.

Role: I adapted a public training recipe from Kaggle, retrained and tested it on four datasets, then wrote the live-input notebook and the Streamlit dashboard.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Testing on voices it has never heard; Pretrained speech model comparison; Prediction API; Live browser microphone; Testing on real call audio.

Q: What is speech emotion recognition? A: Speech emotion recognition is software that listens to a voice clip and guesses the emotion from tone, pitch and energy rather than the words. This project labels seven emotions: angry, disgust, fear, happy, neutral, sad and surprise. It reads numbers that describe the sound from the audio and passes them to a neural network.

Q: How accurate is speech emotion recognition? A: In this project, 93.87% on a random 20% test split of 9,730 samples. That figure does not cover new speakers, because altered copies of one clip can land on both sides of the split. Accuracy on unseen voices is likely to be lower, so a real project would first measure it by splitting speakers apart.

Q: Can it work with my own recordings? A: It can be retrained on your recordings if they are labelled with the emotions you care about. Quality depends on the microphone, the language and the number of speakers. I would first test it on a sample of your audio and report how well it holds.

Q: How much of the speech emotion model did you design yourself? A: The network design is not mine. The training recipe is a public Kaggle notebook, which I adapted and retrained on four datasets. My own work is the testing and its stated limits, the live microphone notebook, the Streamlit dashboard and the saved model files, and I say so plainly on this page.

Q: Why does the repository quote 97.25% when this page says 93.87%? A: The repository README and the notebook's file name quote 97.25%, but the notebook's own output never shows that figure. The saved model scores 93.87% on the 9,730-sample test split, so I report that number, with its caveats. The README figure is not supported by the notebook's output, so this page does not use it.

Q: Does it work in real time from a microphone? A: A notebook records 2.5 seconds at a time, extracts the same features, scales them and prints an emotion, then repeats until stopped. The dashboard can record 1.5 to 5 seconds and shows a bar for each emotion. Neither has been scored for accuracy on live speech, so treat live output as a demo.

Q: How long does it take to train a speech emotion model? A: Here, the 20 training passes took about ten hours in total, roughly half an hour each, and extracting features from all 12,162 clips took about two minutes spread over 20 processor cores. Time depends on the computer and the data, so I would size a new project on a sample first.

# FastAPI OpenTelemetry tracing for an AI backend
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/observable-ai-backend/
Case study: a FastAPI AI server with LLM observability: request IDs in logs, Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry traces in Jaeger.

This FastAPI OpenTelemetry tracing project is an AI server with LLM (large language model) observability built in. A request ID follows every call through logs, metrics and traces (viewed in Jaeger). This means a slow or failing call can be explained from the outside.

A business that puts an AI model behind a support tool, a report or a customer chat needs to know when that feature is slow, failing or quietly using a backup. If the team cannot see inside a request, every complaint turns into guessing: was it the model, the data or its own code? Visibility turns that guessing into a short search.

A good result lets anyone on the team take one complaint, find that exact request, see which step took the time and read the log lines for it. It also shows how heavily the AI servers are used, whether each service is running, and alerts people when something needs attention. This case study covers the request level and the server level, and says which part is which.

Problem: An AI server can return a success code and still be slow, degraded or quietly answering from a different model. Nobody finds out until users complain. By then the cost is already paid: lost trust, a busy support queue and engineers searching logs with no way to tie a complaint to one request. Without counters, nobody can say how often it happens.

What made it hard: Failures that look like success. A missing or slow model can still end in a success code, because a backup path answers. That happened to me during testing, and my first logs and metrics gave no clear sign of it. Finding the slow step. One request passes through a model call, a business action and a second model call. Total time alone does not say which step is slow. Only a step-by-step view does. Telemetry that stays safe and small. Logs can leak customer text and grow fast. Metrics can multiply into thousands of series if a label holds free text. I kept questions and answers out of logs and used a short, fixed set of labels. Seeing the servers, not only requests. A trace explains one call. It does not show whether the machine behind it is short of capacity or a service has stopped. That needs resource use, service status and alerts as well.

Approach: I built a small AI server in FastAPI. For each question, an AI model picks one of three business actions, the action runs, and the model writes a short answer. Every log line and trace step of a request carries the same request ID, and the caller gets it back in the response. A few hand-written metrics count requests, AI response time, tokens (the small pieces of text an AI is billed by) and model fallbacks. Three Groq models are chained, each with its own time limit, and the response carries a "degraded" flag, so a silent fallback becomes visible. At work, I added resource use, service status and alerts to the LLM observability of the company's AI servers.

My part: The whole personal build as sole author: the AI server, its logs, metrics and traces, the Docker Compose setup and the 10 tests. Finding the slow step in a trace, fixing it, and recording the before and after timings. The model chain and fallback counter, added after a real model failure, and the 10-second limit for each model. A written decision log in the repository, including the options I rejected and why. At the company, I added resource use, service status and alerts to the LLM observability of its AI servers, as part of its in-house work.

Context: The personal build is a job-application task on made-up data. It is kept in a private repository and is not a production system. The company work is confidential and sits inside its own systems, so this page shows none of its code, screens or figures. The brief for the personal build asked for an AI backend that can be diagnosed from the outside, with one engineering improvement of my choice.

Architecture: An AI server with an /ask endpoint (a web address the app answers on). An AI model picks one of three business actions: looking up tickets, creating a ticket or running a sales report. The action runs on made-up data, and the model then summarises the result.; A chain of three Groq models, each with a 10-second limit and the library's own retries switched off. If all fail, or no API key is set, a simple keyword router answers and the response is marked "degraded". The service therefore runs with no API key or internet.; One request ID, which is also the trace ID, appears on every JSON log line written during a request, on every trace step and in every /ask response, including errors. The question and the model's answer are deliberately kept out of the logs; only short error details are logged.; Hand-written Prometheus metrics: requests by status code, request time, errors by type, AI call time, tokens, model fallbacks and requests in progress. Labels are never free text, so the stored data stays small.; OpenTelemetry traces are pushed to Jaeger. The web request and the outgoing AI call are traced automatically, and I added spans for routing, the action, the summary and each model call. Health and metrics calls are left out.; A Docker Compose setup starts the app, Jaeger and Prometheus together. Configuration is baked into the images and every host port is a setting, so the stack can be copied to another machine and started the same way.; At the company, resource use, service status and alerts were added to the LLM observability of its AI servers. This part is confidential and is not part of the personal repository..

Design decisions: Tracing as the one big improvement. Of seven options in the brief, I chose OpenTelemetry tracing, and I used the trace ID as the request ID on its log lines and responses. Metrics show that a request was slow and logs show what the code did, but only a trace shows where the time went. One shared ID then links all three. Hand-written logs and metrics. I wrote a short log formatter and picked the metrics myself, instead of using ready-made helper libraries that choose them for you. What to measure should be my decision and easy to explain. A helper library would have hidden the key idea, which is how the trace ID reaches each log line. Fail fast, then try another model. Each model gets a 10-second limit and the provider's own retries are off, so a failing model hands the request to the next one in the chain. The provider's defaults could hold one hung model for up to 180 seconds. With my limit the worst case for one AI call is about 30 seconds across three models. Leave out the large monitoring stack. I declined Grafana, Loki, Tempo and Kubernetes, and used Jaeger and Prometheus on their own screens. The task needed metrics, logs and traces that could be used, not a dashboard product. The extra tools would have added setup time and more containers without adding anything the task needed.

First attempt: I first set a single model, picked from the provider's public model list. On my key that model was not available, yet every request still returned a success code, because the keyword fallback quietly answered. The only sign was a flag in the response, and the log gave just an error class name. What changed: I replaced it with a chain of three models, ordered by the routing speed I measured (121, 492 and 545 milliseconds). I added the provider's error message to the log line and a fallback counter, so a failing first model shows up in monitoring even when users notice nothing.

Results: A deliberately slow lookup (a join over 60,000 made-up tickets) was the largest step in a trace. Once indexed, that step fell from about 15 seconds to under 50 milliseconds, and the whole request from about 16 seconds to under 1 second (captured traces).; 10 automated tests that need no key or internet. They cover the health check, bad input, the unknown-region error, the metrics page, the AI path with a stand-in client, the model chain, the time limit and a provider failure.; A failing first model no longer hides. The fallback counter and the log line record it, and the trace shows a second attempt. When every model fails, the response is flagged "degraded".; A request that took about 12 seconds in testing was explained afterwards from the logs alone: the summary model hung, the 10-second limit fired and the second model answered in under half a second.; At the company, resource use, service status and alerts were added to the LLM observability of the AI servers. The details are confidential and are not published here..

Limits: This is a job-application task, not a production system. The data is made up and held in memory, the slow lookup was planted on purpose, and the timings come from a single test setup, not real traffic. Timings move with machine load: three repeat runs of the slow path took between 17.5 and 27.1 seconds. I report the captured pair as an example, not as an average. The personal build records every trace, defines no alert rules and has no sign-in. A real service would sample traces, add alerts and secure access. The time limit covers AI calls only, not a slow business action. The company work is confidential, so this page shows none of its code, screens or figures. What I can say is limited to what I added: resource use, service status and alerts.

Where this fits: A team running its own AI servers: It wants to see how heavily each model server is used, whether each service is running, and to get an alert before users notice a problem. A product team with an AI feature: Users report slow or odd answers. The team needs to find the exact request and see whether the model, the data or its own code caused the delay. Support and operations leads: They need a request ID that ties one customer complaint to one trace, so they can answer with facts instead of guesses. Teams watching AI cost: Token counts per model and per step show where the spend goes, and whether a backup model is quietly doing most of the work.

Role: Sole author. Design decisions and the options I rejected are logged in the repository.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Dashboards and alerts; Caching and request limits; Sign-in and usage quotas; Routing accuracy test set; Cloud deployment with automatic tests.

Q: What is observability in a FastAPI app? A: Observability means you can tell what a running app is doing from the outside, using logs, metrics and traces. For an AI server this is called LLM observability. A request ID is stamped on every log line and trace step. Prometheus metrics count requests, AI response time and tokens. OpenTelemetry traces in Jaeger show where each request spent its time.

Q: Is this a production system? A: No. The traceable AI server is a job-application task, not a production system. The slow lookup was planted on purpose and the timings come from made-up data. The monitoring I added at work was for real company servers, but it is confidential and not shown here. A real system would need its own traffic, security and hosting decisions.

Q: Can it run without an AI key? A: Yes. With no key set, the server falls back to a simple keyword router and templated answers, and marks every response as degraded. Five of the 10 tests run in that mode. The others use a stand-in for the AI client or check its settings, so none needs a key, an account or internet.

Q: Which part is a personal build and which is company work? A: The traceable AI server is my own job-application build, written alone and kept in a private repository. The company work is separate: I added resource use, service status and alerts to the LLM observability of the company's AI servers. That work is confidential, so I describe it here but show none of its code, screens or figures.

Q: What happens if an AI model fails or hangs? A: A model that is unavailable, rate limited or silent for 10 seconds passes the request to the next of three Groq models. The fallback counter and the log line record each failure, and the response stays normal. If all three fail, simple keyword logic answers and the response is marked "degraded", so the caller knows no AI model wrote it.

Q: Do the logs store customer questions or answers? A: No. The question and the model's answer are deliberately kept out of the logs; only short error details are logged. Each line holds the request ID, the chosen action, row counts and durations. That protects privacy and keeps log volume down. Timing detail for one request lives in its trace.

Q: What does AI server monitoring add to request tracing? A: Tracing explains one request: which step ran and how long it took. Server monitoring watches what sits behind all requests. Resource use shows how much capacity the AI servers are using, service status shows whether each one is running, and alerts tell people when something needs attention. At work I added these to the company's LLM observability.

# Regulatory obligation extraction with AI
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/obligation-management-system/
Case study: an AI service at Claptek that reads circulars, permits and regulations and returns obligations, each with a word-for-word source quote.

This regulatory obligation extraction AI service at Claptek reads regulatory and compliance documents and returns a structured list of obligations. Each one carries a word-for-word source quote, and 97.2% of 1,266 production records link to an exact, highlightable passage in the source PDF.

Banks, lenders and other regulated companies receive circulars, permits and regulations that set out what they must do. Someone has to read each long document, list the duties, say who owns each one and note which clause it comes from. A missed duty can mean a penalty or an audit finding, so the work is slow and careful.

A good result is an evidence-linked obligation list that a compliance officer can check quickly. Each line says who must do what and under which section, and the exact source sentence is highlighted in the original PDF beside it. The reviewer confirms or corrects the list instead of searching through pages to find where each duty came from.

Problem: Compliance teams build obligation lists by hand from long regulatory PDFs, and the page numbers an AI model gives for them cannot be trusted. Hand work is slow and must be repeated whenever a rule changes. Wrong page references send reviewers to the wrong place, so they may stop trusting the list and check everything again, which removes the time saved.

What made it hard: Unreliable page numbers. An AI model can state a page number for each obligation, but those numbers were wrong 56% of the time. A reviewer sent to the wrong page loses trust in the whole list. Long documents. Regulations run to many pages and a model reads only a piece at a time. Duties that cross a page break could be split or lost unless they are joined again. Many kinds of document. Permits, circulars, master directions and know-your-customer rules are written differently. The method had to work on all of them without special code for each type. Measuring fairly. A system built around a few sample documents can look better than it is. I needed a fair test, so I kept some documents apart from those I used while building and compared the same code with one setting changed.

Approach: I built the extraction in four steps. First, the document is split at page boundaries, and a merge step rejoins obligations that cross a break. Second, for each piece an AI language model on Claptek's own servers lists the obligations in a fixed format: an owner (who must act), a category from a fixed list, a risk or control tag and the section, plus the source sentence copied word for word. Third, code searches the PDF for that sentence and reads the page and highlight position from the document itself, instead of trusting a page number from the model. Fourth, a side-by-side preview shows each obligation beside its highlighted evidence.

My part: I designed and built the extraction pipeline: page splitting, the merge step, the fixed-format extraction and the owner and category labels. I built the quote-matching locator that finds each quote in the PDF and works out the page and highlight position, and the side-by-side preview with its scanned-page fallback. I designed and ran the controlled comparison of the second-read step, including the held-back documents and repeated runs. I measured where processing time went, kept the changes that helped, and built cancellable generation. I moved day-to-day development off the remote AI server, so a change could be tested in seconds, and wrote a runbook for other projects to reuse.

Context: The code is in a private client repository, so it cannot be opened for inspection. This page rests on my own work and the measurements I recorded. One colleague helped scope the early intake step. The AI language model runs on Claptek's own servers, and this service calls it.

Architecture: The document is split at page boundaries, and a merge step joins obligations that cross a page break, so a duty is not cut in half.; For each piece, an AI language model hosted on Claptek's own servers extracts the obligations. It records each in a fixed format: an owner, a category from a fixed list, a risk or control tag and the section, so output stays consistent from one document to the next.; A locator finds each word-for-word quote in the PDF, using PyMuPDF (a PDF reading library), and reads the page number and highlight position from the document itself. I tested it on a set of reference records before connecting it to the live pipeline.; A side-by-side PDF preview (pdf.js, a browser PDF viewer) highlights the evidence for each obligation. For scanned pages that pdf.js cannot draw, the preview falls back to an image of the page at matching scale, so highlights stay in place.; Generation can be cancelled, which frees the model's memory and keeps the extracts already finished, so a long run resumes instead of restarting.; A second-read step, so far only tested in a controlled comparison and not yet in the live service, quotes the sentences that impose duties, drops every quote that is not found word for word in the PDF, and writes records from what is left.; A FastAPI backend (a Python web framework) serves the extraction, a React screen shows the list and the preview, and Docker packages the whole service for easy installation on a server..

Design decisions: Find the quote instead of trusting the page. I ask the model to copy the source sentence word for word, then let code find that sentence in the PDF and read off the page and highlight position. The model quoted text well but stated page numbers badly: its page numbers were wrong 56% of the time. Matching text is exact work for code, so each job goes to the tool that does it best. Measure each speed-up before keeping it. I profiled where processing time went, tested each proposed speed-up and kept only those that helped. Running two copies of the model side by side gave no net gain, so I did not use it. Measurement showed the limit was how fast the machine can read the model's memory, which a second copy cannot widen. The changes that did help cut a six-document run from 80.4 to 60.0 minutes. Check every quote against the source. In the second-read step I tested, a first pass only quotes sentences that impose duties. Each quote is checked word for word against the PDF and dropped if it does not match. A model can produce a plausible sentence that is not in the document. Dropping every unmatched quote lets the extra pass add coverage without adding invented quotes. Test fairly before claiming a gain. I compared the same code with one setting changed, on documents kept apart from those I used while building the step, and repeated identical runs to see how much results vary by chance. One run on the documents used while building can flatter a result. Measuring the run-to-run spread shows which gains are real and which are noise.

First attempt: The AI model stated the page number for each obligation. Checked against the source, those page numbers had been wrong 56% of the time, so a reviewer following them would often land on the wrong page. What changed: I asked for a word-for-word quote instead, and wrote code that finds the quote in the PDF and reads off the page and highlight position. Now 97.2% of 1,266 production records link to an exact, highlightable passage.

Results: 97.2% of 1,266 production records link to an exact, highlightable passage in the source PDF. Before this, the page numbers the AI model stated had been wrong 56% of the time.; 100% of records carry a word-for-word source quote, so a reviewer can check each record against the passage the model quoted.; In a controlled test of an extra reading step (not yet live), recall (the share of obligations found) rose from 32% to 69% for Basel III rules and from 69% to 82% for KYC (know-your-customer) rules, on documents kept apart from those used while building.; Processing time for a six-document benchmark fell from 80.4 to 60.0 minutes, after I measured where the time went and kept only the changes that helped.; The same process reads permits, circulars and regulations with no domain-specific code..

Limits: About 2.8% of production records were not matched to an exact passage, and a person should still review the whole list. Those records still carry the quote the model gave, so a reviewer can search for it by hand. The recall gains come from a controlled test of an extra reading step that is not yet in the live service. I report Basel III banking rules and KYC rules only, and have not measured data protection, safety or tax rules. A reviewer may still find a duplicate record or a duty assigned to the wrong party, so a person should check the whole list. I have not built support for documents in other languages, or for translation. Lists are also not versioned, so a revised circular needs a fresh run and a manual comparison.

Where this fits: Compliance teams in banks and lenders: Turn a new circular or master direction into a list of evidence-linked compliance obligations, each tied to the sentence it came from. Environmental, health and safety teams: List the conditions and limits in a permit, with each one linked to its source clause, so site managers know what they must do. Legal and policy teams: List the duties set out in long policies or agreements, each linked to its clause. I would first test the method on a sample of your documents. Internal audit and risk teams: Start control testing from a structured, evidence-linked list of duties, then check that each duty has a control and a test.

Role: Primary engineer at Claptek. I wrote nearly all of the code; one colleague helped scope the early intake step.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Versioned lists and change tracking; Searchable document library; Accuracy scoring; Reviewer approval workflow; Speed dashboards.

Q: How do you extract obligations from regulatory documents? A: Split the document into pieces, then ask an AI language model to list each obligation and quote the source word for word. Code then finds that quote in the PDF to work out the page and highlight position, instead of trusting the page numbers the model gives. A person should still review the list.

Q: How do you keep the citations accurate? A: The AI returns a word-for-word quote, and code then finds that quote in the PDF to work out the page and highlight position. In the production data I measured, 97.2% of 1,266 records were located exactly. This replaced page numbers the model had often got wrong.

Q: Does it only work for one kind of regulation? A: No. It is not tied to one domain. The same process has read environmental permits, banking master directions, Basel III circulars and KYC rules without any domain-specific code. Other documents could work too, though I would first check results on a sample.

Q: What counts as an obligation in a regulatory document? A: An obligation is a duty the document places on someone: who must do what, and under which section. Examples are a duty to report, to keep records or to stay within a limit. The service lists each one with its owner, a category and a risk or control tag.

Q: What does the 97.2% figure actually measure? A: It measures how many of 1,266 production records could be linked to an exact passage in the source PDF, found by matching the model's word-for-word quote. Every record has a quote. The remaining 2.8% were not matched to an exact passage, so a reviewer should check those by hand.

Q: Does it replace the compliance reviewer? A: No. It gives a reviewer a head start: a structured list in which each duty sits beside its highlighted source sentence, so checking should be faster. A person should still review the list and correct mistakes, such as a duty placed on the wrong party. The aim is faster, better-evidenced review, not unchecked automation.

Q: Where does the AI model run when it reads my documents? A: In this project the AI language model runs on Claptek's own servers, not on an online AI service. For other similar projects, I would check what hardware is available, because larger models need stronger machines, and then run the model where the documents are allowed to stay.

# AI audit finding generator and drafting engine
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/ams-ai-finding-engine/
Case study: an AI audit finding generator at Claptek. It drafts three versions of each finding from checklist notes, and code checks block invented facts.

The AI audit finding generator is a standalone service at Claptek that turns short audit checklist notes into draft findings, three versions each. Code-level checks block any invented figure, date or owner, so the AI cannot add facts that were not in the auditor's note.

Audit teams record what they find in short checklist notes. Each note must become a formal finding with a title, a description, a recommendation and a severity rating. That write-up is slow, and a vague or wrong one leaves the people responsible unsure what to do. Faster, steadier drafting can give auditors time back for testing controls.

A good result is an auditor who types a short note and receives three draft findings in seconds, worded like earlier findings from the same bank. No draft adds a figure, date or owner that the auditor did not write. A person reviews every draft, and a whole checklist can be drafted in one pass.

Problem: Auditors spend hours turning terse checklist notes into well-formed findings. Simple AI drafting tends to invent figures and names. Both cost the business, because slow write-ups take time from real audit work. An invented figure, date or owner is worse, because someone may act on it or trust the report less.

What made it hard: Models invent details. Asked to write a finding, a language model fills gaps with plausible figures, dates and names. In an audit, one invented fact can mislead the people who must act on it. Thin, uneven notes. Checklist notes are short, and each bank words things its own way. The service had to write a complete finding from very little, in the style of that bank's earlier findings. A very slow response. At one point a single request took 7.9 minutes, which no auditor will wait for. The cause was buried in the way the system called the AI models, so I had to find it by testing. Fitting a live product. The drafting had to work inside an audit product that another team owns, built with Spring Boot and React. The feature also had to be easy for that team to adopt.

Approach: I built the drafting engine as a standalone FastAPI service (a Python web framework). An auditor's checklist note arrives with its verdict, and simple checks run before any AI time is spent. The service then finds similar past findings to use as writing examples. An AI language model that runs on Claptek's own servers writes the title, description, recommendation and severity, in three versions: short, balanced and detailed. Hard checks in code follow: any draft containing a figure, date or owner that is not in the auditor's note is rejected. Bulk mode drafts a whole workbook into a reviewable grid, and the client's audit product shows the three versions on its own edit screen.

My part: I designed and built the whole drafting service: the data formats, the search for past findings, the drafting steps, the code checks and the three-version output. I built bulk mode: spreadsheet upload, column mapping, the reviewable grid, the export and the written summary report. I built the connection to the client's Java and React audit product, including the database query that gathers each item's details and the drafting action on its edit screen. I found the cause of the slowdown, fixed it and ran the four-model comparison of speed and draft quality. I audited my own evaluation scripts, found measurement faults that had inflated the scores, and corrected them.

Context: The service lives in a private client repository, so the code cannot be opened for inspection. This page rests on my own work, the test results and the measurements I took. The audit product itself, with its Spring Boot and React code and its database, already existed and is owned by a separate product team. Other engineers built its other AI features. The AI language models run on Claptek's own servers, and this service calls them.

Architecture: One settings file per bank holds that bank's categories, example findings, pass and fail wording and required fields, so one codebase serves several banks.; Simple checks on the auditor's note run first, before any AI time is spent. A search step then finds similar past findings by keyword matching (TF-IDF, a keyword-weighting method) and passes them to the model as writing examples.; An AI language model on Claptek's own servers writes the title, description, recommendation and severity, using the auditor's note and the retrieved examples.; Code-level checks run on every reply. A draft is rejected if it holds a figure, date or owner that is not in the auditor's note. With no usable note, the service returns an outline with no specific facts for the auditor to complete.; Three versions of every finding: short, balanced and detailed, so the auditor can pick one and edit it.; Bulk mode: the user uploads a checklist workbook and maps its columns in the browser. Each row is drafted into a reviewable grid where it can be accepted, edited or rejected, then exported. A written summary report groups the findings by theme.; The client's audit product, built with Spring Boot (a Java framework) and React (a web screen library), gains a drafting action on its edit screen. Its backend gathers the item's details with one database query and sends them to this service, and the screen shows the three versions inline..

Design decisions: Check in code, not in the prompt. I enforce the rule that every figure, date and owner must appear in the auditor's note with a check in code, not only with an instruction in the prompt. An instruction is a request that a model can ignore. A check in code rejects the draft every time, so the guarantee does not depend on how the model behaves that day. Measure the slowdown before fixing it. When requests took 7.9 minutes, I tested the AI model server directly instead of relying on its documentation, found the hidden extra processing, and compared four candidate models. Guessing at fixes wastes time. Direct tests showed what the server really did. Once the hidden processing was off, time per request fell to 16.9 seconds and accuracy stayed unchanged. Let the AI label, let code count. In the summary report, the AI only labels each finding with a theme and an owner. Code does all the counting, and an owner label is accepted only if it appears in that row's own recommendation. Charts built from AI-written numbers can look right and be wrong. Here code does the counting from the spreadsheet itself, and the AI only supplies the labels. Reuse the product's own sign-in. I made the drafting action use the audit product's existing sign-in, so it adds no new login to manage. Drafts are built from confidential audit data. Reusing the product's existing access control keeps a single set of access rules to maintain.

Results: 0 invented facts across 27 checked draft versions, measured on real audit notes: none contained a figure, date or owner that was missing from the auditor's note.; Time per request fell from 7.9 minutes to 16.9 seconds, about 28 times faster. The cause was hidden extra processing in the way the system called the AI models. I fixed it and compared four candidate models, and accuracy stayed unchanged.; 313 automated tests pass, and the code passes style and type checks.; The client's audit product team adopted the feature the day after handover. I had handed it over with a self-contained integration guide.; A reviewer gets three versions of each finding and can accept, edit or reject every row of a bulk run..

Limits: A person must still review every finding. The checks stop invented figures, dates and owners, but they cannot judge whether the wording or the severity rating is right. The result of zero invented facts comes from 27 draft versions, which is a small sample, and the 16.9 seconds was measured on Claptek's own servers. I would measure both again on your notes and your hardware. Finding similar past findings uses keyword matching, so it can miss an example that says the same thing in different words. Today the service does not record who accepted or edited a draft, and it has no user roles of its own.

Where this fits: Internal audit teams: Turn short checklist observations into formal findings in the house style, with an auditor reviewing every draft before it is issued. Compliance and risk teams: Draft control-testing results or exception notes from a few lines of input, where every figure, date and owner must come from the source. IT service and operations teams: Turn terse incident or ticket notes into clear reports, with a check that the AI adds no times, names or numbers that nobody entered. Inspection and quality teams: Write up site or process inspections as standard reports, where each reading and date must match what the inspector recorded.

Role: Sole engineer at Claptek. I built it end to end. That covers the data formats, the drafting process, the safety checks, bulk mode and the connection to the client's Java and React product.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Draft-quality scoring; Reviewer feedback loop; Speed and cost dashboards; Better search of past findings; User roles and activity history.

Q: Can AI write audit findings without making things up? A: Yes, when code checks every draft. Every figure, date or owner in a draft must appear word for word in the auditor's own note. A check rejects any draft that adds one. Across 27 checked draft versions it produced no invented facts, though a person still reviews each finding.

Q: Could the same approach work on my reports or tickets? A: The method is not specific to audit. It finds relevant evidence, uses an AI model hosted on your own machines and checks the output in code. I would first test it on a sample of your own documents to see how well it holds.

Q: Why did drafting get faster, from 7.9 minutes to 16.9 seconds? A: The cause was hidden extra processing: the AI model was doing long, hidden reasoning before each answer. I found it by testing the model server directly, fixed it and compared four candidate models on speed and draft quality. Time per request fell from 7.9 minutes to 16.9 seconds, about 28 times faster, with accuracy unchanged.

Q: What happens when the auditor's note is too short? A: The service does not guess. When there is no usable note, it returns an outline with no specific figures, dates or owners, and the auditor completes it. This stops a plausible but made-up story from being presented as fact, and it matches the rule enforced by the code checks.

Q: Can it draft a whole audit checklist spreadsheet at once? A: Yes. In bulk mode the user uploads a checklist workbook and maps its columns. Every row is drafted into a grid that looks like a spreadsheet, with all three versions of each finding. Reviewers accept, edit or reject each row, export the result and get a written summary report.

Q: How does it fit into an existing audit product? A: The drafting engine is its own FastAPI service. A drafting action on the audit product's edit screen has the product's backend gather the item's details and send them across, and the three versions appear on the same screen. I handed it over with a self-contained integration guide, and the client's team adopted it the day after handover.

Q: Can it follow our own audit categories and wording? A: Yes. Each bank has its own settings file holding its categories, example findings, pass and fail wording and required fields, so one codebase serves several banks. The search step also shows the model similar past findings, which helps drafts follow earlier house style. I would build the settings from your own past findings.

# Text-to-SQL LLM assistant for core banking
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/core-banking-text-to-sql/
Case study: a text-to-SQL assistant at Claptek turning plain questions into Oracle queries over a 1,628-table bank database, on the bank's own servers.

This text-to-SQL LLM (AI language model) assistant at Claptek runs on the bank's own servers. It turns plain-language reporting questions into working Oracle database queries (SQL) over a large core-banking database. My part was the accuracy measurement and the self-correction loop.

Banks and other large organisations keep their records in databases that can hold more than a thousand tables. In some of them only a few specialists can write SQL, the language used to read those tables, so each new report waits in a queue. A tool that turns a plain question into a correct query removes that wait, but only if people can trust what it returns.

A good result is an on-premise text-to-SQL assistant: it runs on the bank's own servers, so the bank's data stays inside the bank. It finds the right tables, writes a query that runs and returns the right accounts. Its quality is measured by running its queries on a real database, so a manager can see how often it is right before relying on it.

Problem: The project's simple scoring rated the query writer at about 93% good. Actually running its queries showed that the share returning exactly the right rows was close to zero. Those scores checked whether the right tables were found and whether expected code values appeared in the query text, not whether the query returned the right rows. A team that trusts such a number ships wrong or empty reports and fixes the wrong things.

What made it hard: A very large database. A layout of 1,628 tables is too large to show a model in full for every question, so the few tables a question needs must be found first. Scores that flatter. A query can look right and still return the wrong rows, or none. Only running it and comparing its rows with those of a query known to be correct shows the truth. Invented code values. Many columns hold fixed codes, not words. A model that guesses a code writes a filter that looks right but matches nothing. Strict client limits. The model had to run on the bank's own servers. A larger model and retraining were not allowed, so any gain had to come from how the system uses the model it had.

Approach: I built the measurement first: a test that runs each generated query on a real database and compares the returned rows with a known-correct query. It scores strict row matches and also the recall and precision of the accounts returned. Then I added a retry loop, limited to two passes. When a query fails or returns no rows, the model is shown the real error and real values from the database, and asked to fix it. A glossary of real code values in the prompt makes filters use values that exist. The client ruled out a larger model and any retraining, so the gains had to come from the pipeline itself.

My part: The accuracy test that scores every generated query by running it and checking the rows it returns against the known-correct answer. The scoring: strict row matching, plus recall and precision on the accounts a query returns, so partial success is visible. The self-correction loop, limited to two passes, that shows the model the real error and real column values and asks for a fix. The glossary of real code values added to the prompt, so filters use values that exist in the database. Repeatable test runs: generation fixed at zero randomness, plus setup notes and a launcher so the pipeline could be run and measured on an ordinary developer machine.

Context: A Claptek teammate built the table search over 1,628 tables, the query safety guard and the test data. I worked on the accuracy and correction side of a two-person effort. No model was trained or tuned, and none was swapped. The client ruled out a larger model and retraining. This is confidential client work. The database layout, the bank's data and the code stay private, so this page describes the design and the measured results only.

Architecture: Table search, built by my teammate: it finds the right tables for each question in a core-banking database of 1,628 tables, using methods that include keyword search (BM25).; A language model (LLM) hosted on the bank's own servers with vLLM, a model-serving program, writes the Oracle query from the question and the chosen tables.; The query safety guard, built by my teammate with a SQL parser (sqlglot), checks each generated query before it runs. The test data was also my teammate's work.; The accuracy test, built by me, executes every generated query against a live database and compares its rows with those of a known-correct query. It reports strict row matches, accounts found (recall) and the correct share of results (precision).; The self-correction loop, built by me and limited to two passes: when a query errors or returns no rows, the model sees the real error and real column values, then revises the query.; A glossary of real code values from the database is added to the prompt, so filters use values that actually exist.; Hosted entirely on the bank's own servers, model included, so no outside AI service is involved. Generation is fixed at zero randomness to keep test runs repeatable..

Design decisions: Score by running the queries. I chose to judge quality by running each generated query on a real database, over scoring table matches and code strings in the query text. Stand-in scores read about 93% while the share of queries returning exactly the right rows was close to zero. Only the rows a query returns show whether it does its job. Fix the loop, not the model. I chose a self-correction loop, limited to two passes, over asking for a larger model or retraining, which the client had ruled out. The database itself tells the model what went wrong: a real error, or no rows. The loop is capped at two passes, so a hopeless query cannot retry forever. Show the model real code values. I chose to add a glossary of real code values to the prompt, over letting the model guess which codes a column holds. Guessed codes look plausible but match nothing. With real values in front of it, the model writes filters that can find accounts. Fix randomness for repeatable scores. I chose to set the model's generation to zero randomness, over leaving it free, so test runs stay repeatable. With random variation, a gain of a few points cannot be told from noise. Repeatable runs let each change be judged on its own.

Results: After the self-correction loop was added, accounts found (recall) rose from 34% to 54% and the correct share of results (precision) from 19% to 27%, with no model change and no retraining. Both come from running the queries on a real database.; 100% of 40 held-out test queries (kept apart from the ones used while building) were valid against the live database layout.; Stand-in scoring had put quality at about 93%. Running the queries put the exact-match rate close to zero, so every later gain is measured against a realistic baseline.; Generation is fixed at zero randomness to keep test runs repeatable, so a change in score points to a change in the system rather than to chance.; The whole pipeline, including the model, runs on the bank's own servers, so no data, prompt or usage record leaves the machine..

Limits: At 54% accounts found and 27% correct share of results, the output is a draft to review, not a finished report. A person should check a generated query before relying on its numbers. Valid means a query fits the live database layout (100% of 40 held-out queries). It does not prove the rows are right. Recall and precision are the measures of that. The figures come from one database with a core-banking layout, loaded with test data, and a prepared set of test questions. Another database or kind of question would need its own accuracy test before the numbers are trusted. The gains came from how the system uses the model, inside the client's limits of no larger model and no retraining. I cannot say how far a bigger or tuned model would go.

Where this fits: Bank reporting teams: Analysts wait for a data team to write each query. Text-to-SQL for banking may shorten that wait, if the queries are checked and the assistant runs on the bank's own servers. Audit and compliance teams: Reviewers want quick answers, such as which accounts meet a condition, drawn from live data, with the query shown so the answer can be checked and repeated. Companies with a very large old database: Hundreds or thousands of tables and few people who know them. Table search plus query writing can help, and an accuracy test shows whether it is good enough to use. Teams with a text-to-SQL prototype: A demo looks good on simple scores, but nobody has run the queries. An accuracy test on real rows shows the true quality, and a correction loop may lift it without a new model.

Role: A focused part of a two-person team at Claptek. I built the accuracy test and the self-correction loop. My teammate built the table search, the query safety guard and the test data.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Automatic accuracy checks on every change; Table search by meaning; Explained results with charts; Feedback that builds the answer key; Speed and failure tracking.

Q: What is text to SQL? A: Text to SQL means asking a database a question in everyday words and having an AI language model write the SQL query that answers it. The query is then run against the database. The hard parts are choosing the right tables and checking that the query is correct, which is why this project measures results by running queries.

Q: Is text to SQL safe for a bank database? A: It can be, with controls. Here the AI model runs on the bank's own servers, so no data, prompt or usage record leaves the machine. A query safety guard also checks queries before they run. My teammate built that guard; I built the accuracy test that compares returned rows with a correct query.

Q: How do you measure whether the generated query is right? A: By running it. The accuracy test executes the generated query on a real database and compares the rows with a known-correct query. Recall is the share of the right accounts the query returns; precision is the share of returned accounts that are right. These replaced simple scores that had overstated quality.

Q: Does any data leave the machine? A: No. The assistant runs fully on the bank's own servers, so no data, prompt or usage record leaves the machine. The AI model is hosted there too, so no online AI service is involved. For another project, the first step is to check that the servers are strong enough to run the model.

Q: Why did the first accuracy score say 93% when real accuracy was far lower? A: The first scores checked stand-ins: whether the right tables were found and whether the expected code values appeared in the query text. A query can pass both checks and still return wrong or empty results. Running the queries on a real database showed that exact row matches were close to zero, so I replaced the stand-ins.

Q: Which parts of the text-to-SQL assistant did you build yourself? A: I built the accuracy test and the self-correction loop, plus the code-value glossary in the prompt. A Claptek teammate built the table search, the query safety guard and the test data. It was a focused part of a two-person effort.

Q: Did you retrain or replace the AI model to raise accuracy? A: No. The client allowed no larger model and no retraining, so the model stayed as it was. The gain came from the self-correction loop: when a query failed or returned nothing, the model saw the real error and real column values and tried again, up to two passes. Recall rose from 34% to 54%.

# AI scam honeypot that keeps scammers talking
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/agentic-honeypot/
Case study: an AI that plays an easily fooled target, keeps scammers talking and records the UPI payment IDs, links and phone numbers they reveal.

This AI scam honeypot is a counter-scam system co-built with Prasanna Patil. An AI plays an easily fooled victim, keeps scammers talking and records the UPI payment IDs, links and phone numbers they reveal. A rule-based selector changes its style as scam risk grows, and a live dashboard shows what it collects.

Banks, payment apps, telecom firms and messaging platforms face the same pattern. Scammers message many people at once, and each reply, click or payment costs a real person money and costs the business support time and trust. Blocking one number changes little, because the scammer moves to the next. What is usually missing is a record of how the scam works.

A good result is a safe place where a scammer can be kept talking for as long as possible, while the business collects the payment IDs, links and phone numbers the scammer shares. That record can feed block lists and investigations. This case study covers a hackathon prototype of that idea, built with a co-builder, and says clearly who built which part.

Problem: A blocked scammer just tries the next number, and nobody learns how the scam works. A bot that keeps scammers busy protects real people for as long as the chat lasts and leaves a record of exactly what the scammers ask for. Without that record, a fraud team may learn about a scam only after someone reports a loss.

What made it hard: Staying believable. A scammer may test whether a bot is on the other end. The persona must reply in short, casual messages, stay in character for many turns and never admit to being an AI. Hostile and abusive input. The other side is a scammer, so messages may try to hijack the AI, for example with "ignore previous instructions", or flood the server. A cheap first line of defence must act before any message reaches the model. Messy payment details. UPI IDs, links and phone numbers can be written in many forms, such as a link with no "http" or a number with spaces. A pattern wide enough to catch them will also catch some look-alikes. Two builders, one codebase. The 18 build commits in the shared history fall on two days. Two people worked on one codebase, so I used separate branches that were merged back through pull requests.

Approach: The system is a FastAPI service with a React dashboard. It scores every incoming message for scam signals. Separately, a rule-based selector sets the bot's style: passive at first, vulnerable once a risk level (raised by shouting or very short messages) passes a limit, and stalling once enough details are collected. A persona prompt drives an AI model on Groq, which writes each reply from the last 10 messages. Pattern matching pulls out payment and contact details, and the live dashboard shows them. Prasanna Patil wrote the first version. I added the safety layer, moved the AI to Groq and rewrote the persona prompts and the link and phone patterns.

My part: A filter for prompt-injection phrases that answers with a canned confused reply, and a request limiter of 1 per second per visitor with bursts of 5. Moving the reply model from Gemini to Groq, including how the last 10 messages are passed to it. Rewriting the persona prompts, and the patterns that pick out phone numbers and web addresses. Small dashboard changes: it now sends the access key and no longer names a model, and its build tools moved to Vite 6.

Context: Prasanna Patil wrote the first version: scam scoring, the style selector, conversation memory, the detail extractor, the API and the first dashboard, plus the Docker setup and the README. It is a hackathon prototype. In the shared commit history, 18 of the 19 changes fall on two days; the last, a licence file, came months later.

Architecture: Intake, from Prasanna's first version. A FastAPI endpoint takes a conversation ID and a message, as text or a small JSON object, and needs an access key in a request header. Interactive API documentation (Scalar) is served alongside it.; Safety layer, added by me. A filter checks for five known injection phrases and, on a match, sends a canned confused reply and does not store the message. A limiter gives each visitor address 1 request per second, with bursts of 5, and refuses the rest with HTTP 429.; Scam scoring, from Prasanna's first version. 21 keyword patterns, such as lottery, tax, UPI and arrest, each add 0.2 to a message's score. At 0.7 or more the conversation is flagged, and the flag stays. The bot replies either way.; Style selection, from Prasanna's first version. A rule-based selector picks one of four styles: passive on the first message, engaged after that, vulnerable once a running risk level passes 0.6, and stalling once more than three details are collected. Shouting or very short messages raise the risk level.; Persona, memory and model, shared. Each conversation is kept in server memory under its ID. A persona prompt that I rewrote, plus the current style, goes to a model hosted on Groq with the last 10 messages. I moved this step from Gemini to Groq.; Detail extraction, first version by Prasanna, link and phone patterns widened by me. Patterns pick UPI IDs, links and phone numbers out of each incoming message. Each record keeps its type, value, a fixed confidence (0.9, 0.95 and 0.8) and the turn it appeared in.; Dashboard and delivery. Prasanna built the React dashboard, the Docker setup and the README. The dashboard shows the chat, the status, the current style, the collected details and the matched signals. I made small changes to it..

Design decisions: Answer injection attempts with a canned reply. When a message contains an injection phrase, the bot sends one of four canned confused replies and skips the AI model, instead of returning an error. The injected text never reaches the model, and the other side still gets an ordinary reply, not an error. A keyword list is only a first line of defence, as the limits section says. A token bucket for the request limit. I used a token bucket (an allowance that refills over time) for each visitor address: 1 request per second, with bursts of 5. A quick burst of messages passes, but a sustained flood does not. The limiter is small, needs no extra service, and refused requests get the standard HTTP 429 answer. A short, casual, slightly lazy persona. I rewrote the persona prompt so the bot plays a human, replies in one or two casual sentences, never admits to being an AI and is not too eager. The active persona is a student short of cash and keen on quick money; an elderly persona is defined but not used. The prompt aims for a believable young person, sceptical by default, which suits keeping a scammer talking. Wider patterns for links and numbers. I widened the link pattern to catch web addresses without "http", and added capture of 10-digit and country-code phone numbers. A strict pattern misses bare addresses and plain numbers. The cost is false matches, such as an email's domain read as a link or any ten-digit number read as a phone number, so the details are leads for a person to check, not verified facts.

Results: The bot's style changes automatically: passive on the first message, engaged from the second, vulnerable once the risk level passes 0.6, and stalling once more than three details are collected.; UPI IDs, links and phone numbers are stored as structured threat records: type, value, a fixed confidence (0.9, 0.95 and 0.8) and the turn found. These confidence values are set in the code, not measured accuracy.; Each visitor address is limited to 1 request per second, with bursts of 5. A request over the limit gets HTTP 429.; The persona sees the last 10 messages for each reply, while the server keeps the whole conversation in memory under its ID.; A live dashboard shows warning signals, the current style and the details collected, next to the chat window where the tester plays the scammer.; Contribution record: of 19 changes in the shared history, I wrote 4 and merged 4 pull requests. The other 11 are Prasanna's, counted from the commit log..

Limits: Detection is keyword based, not semantic. A message needs at least four of the 21 patterns to be flagged, so honest messages can be flagged and new tricks missed. It has not been measured on labelled conversations. The injection filter is a keyword list, so it is a first line of defence, not a full defence. The limiter and the conversation memory live in server memory, so they reset on restart and do not work across several servers. Patterns can misread: an email address can be recorded as a UPI ID, and a repeated detail is stored again each time. The collected details are not sent anywhere, so there is no report to a bank or an authority. This is a hackathon prototype. The repository has no automated test suite, the sample access key and server address are written into the demo code, and if the AI provider fails the reply is an error message.

Where this fits: A bank or payments fraud team: It wants a safe decoy that scammers can be steered to, so it can collect the payment IDs, links and numbers they use as leads for block lists and investigations. A messaging or telecom trust team: It wants to study how scam scripts unfold, what scammers ask for and how long they stay engaged, without putting a real customer in the conversation. A university or security research lab: It needs a controlled decoy to study scammer behaviour, with each message, the bot's style and the collected details visible on one dashboard. A consumer awareness team: It wants real examples of how current scams escalate, to train staff and warn customers. That would need conversations saved to a database, which this prototype does not do.

Role: Co-author with Prasanna Patil. I added the filter that blocks prompt-injection attempts (tricks that try to hijack the AI) and the request limiter. I moved the AI from Gemini to Groq. I also rewrote the persona prompts and detail-extraction patterns, and reworked parts of the dashboard. Prasanna wrote the first version, the Docker setup and the README.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): A learned scam detector with scoring; Memory and tools for the agent; Searchable conversation store; Attack-testing suite; Tracking and analytics dashboards.

Q: What is an AI honeypot? A: An AI honeypot is a decoy that looks like an easy target, so attackers waste their time on it and reveal how they work. Here an AI persona plays a victim in a chat and keeps a scammer talking. It records the payment IDs, links and phone numbers the scammer shares, ready for study.

Q: How do you create an AI agent? A: Give the AI a clear job, a way to read the situation and rules for what it may do. In this project each message is scored for scam signals. A rule-based selector picks one of four styles, and an AI persona on Groq writes the reply. Pattern matching then saves the details it collects.

Q: Who built which part? A: It was co-built with Prasanna Patil. Prasanna wrote the first version, the Docker setup and the README. I added the injection filter and the request limiter, moved the AI from Gemini to Groq, and rewrote the persona prompts and the link and phone patterns. Of the 19 changes in the shared history, I wrote 4 and merged 4.

Q: How well does it resist prompt injection? A: It has a keyword filter for five phrases, such as "ignore previous instructions", and a request limiter. On a match, the bot sends a canned reply and the text never reaches the model. That is a first line of defence, not a complete solution, because a determined attacker can reword a trick. A real project would add attack tests.

Q: What details does the honeypot record from a scammer? A: It records UPI IDs, links and phone numbers found in the scammer's messages. Each record keeps its type, the value, a fixed confidence level and the turn where it appeared. It does not look for bank account numbers or card numbers. Records stay in server memory until the server restarts, and the dashboard shows them as they arrive.

Q: How does the bot remember a conversation? A: Each conversation is stored in server memory under its ID, with every message, the scam score, the current style and the details found. For each reply the AI model sees the last 10 messages. Because the store is in memory, a restart clears everything. A real version would use a database.

Q: Does the honeypot report scammers anywhere? A: No. Apart from the request to the AI model, it makes no outgoing calls. The collected details stay in the reply it returns, in server memory and on the dashboard. Sending them to a fraud team, a block list or a case system would be an addition I can build if a project needs it.
