# WhatsApp AI agent that replies in the background
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/whatsapp-ai-agent-platform/
Case study: a WhatsApp AI agent backend built in an internship for a client. FastAPI, Redis and Celery send AI replies in the background.

This WhatsApp AI agent platform is a backend I built during an internship for a client. It receives customer messages through a webhook, tracks each user and writes AI replies in the background with Redis and Celery, so the AI never blocks the web request. Conversations are saved in PostgreSQL. The repository is private.

Many businesses talk to customers on WhatsApp: questions, bookings and updates. An AI agent can answer the routine messages, but only if it replies without making people wait, remembers who it is talking to and lets a human know when a person is needed. Without that, the chat turns into a slow, forgetful inbox.

A good result is a backend that receives each message, keeps a record of every user and conversation, and writes the AI reply in the background. Customers get automatic messages, staff get alerts, and the web layer stays free to take the next message. This project is that kind of backend, built for a client.

Problem: A business that talks to customers on WhatsApp must receive every message, match it to the right customer and answer without making anyone wait. An AI model takes longer to reply than a web request should wait. If the reply is written inside that request, slow answers hold up the service. Without saved history, the agent forgets the customer, repeats questions and wastes staff time.

What made it hard: AI replies are slow. A language model takes longer to answer than a web request should wait, so the reply cannot be written inside the request that receives the message. Remembering each customer. Every message arrives on its own. The platform must match it to the right user and bring back their state and history, so the conversation continues across sessions. Reliable background work. Moving the AI work out of the request needs a queue and workers. Jobs must be handled reliably, so a reply can be written after the request has ended. Two messaging providers. Customer messages and operator alerts rely on the Meta WhatsApp Business API and Twilio, so the platform has to work with both side by side.

Approach: I built a backend (a message receiver, a job queue, background workers and a database) in Python with FastAPI. The receiver takes each WhatsApp message through a webhook, which is a web address that the messaging service calls, and tracks the user. The AI work goes onto a Redis and Celery job queue, and a worker writes the reply, so the AI never blocks the web request. PostgreSQL keeps user state and the full conversation history. The Meta WhatsApp Business API and Twilio carry customer messages and operator alerts.

My part: The FastAPI backend that receives WhatsApp messages through a webhook and tracks each user. The background reply path: Redis and Celery workers that write the AI reply, so it never blocks the web request. The PostgreSQL storage for user state, conversation context and the full conversation history. The connections to the Meta WhatsApp Business API and Twilio for automatic customer messages and operator alerts.

Context: This was a client project during an internship, and the repository is private, so I cannot show code, screenshots or the client's name. The AI models and the WhatsApp and Twilio services are third-party tools that I connected to. I did not build or train them.

Architecture: A FastAPI webhook receives each incoming WhatsApp message and hands the slow work on, so the web request is never held up by the AI; User state tracking: the platform keeps a record of each user in PostgreSQL, so every new message is matched to the right person and their earlier context; A Redis and Celery job queue runs the AI work in background workers, built for reliable asynchronous processing, so a reply being written never blocks the web request; The AI agent writes each reply in a worker, using the saved conversation context, so interactions stay personal and continue across sessions; The full conversation history is stored in PostgreSQL, so a conversation can be picked up again in a later session; The Meta WhatsApp Business API and Twilio carry the automatic customer messages and the alerts sent to human operators.

Design decisions: Reply in the background, not in the request. I used Redis and Celery so the AI reply is written by a background worker, and the web request that receives the message does not wait for it. AI models are slow compared with a web request. Keeping the AI off the request thread means a slow reply never blocks the receiver. I chose Redis and Celery for reliable background processing. Keep state and history in PostgreSQL. I stored each user's state, the conversation context and the full history in a PostgreSQL database. A database lets the AI agent carry on a conversation across sessions and keeps interactions personal. Data held only in memory would be lost whenever the program restarted. Use both Meta and Twilio. I connected the Meta WhatsApp Business API and Twilio, for automatic customer messages and for alerts to human operators. The aim was multi-channel messaging: customers get automatic replies and notifications, and operators can be alerted.

Results: It receives a customer's WhatsApp message through a webhook and tracks the user it came from; It replies in the background: the AI reply is written by a Celery worker, so the web request that received the message is not held up; It saves the user's state and the full conversation history in PostgreSQL, so the agent can continue a conversation in a later session; I connected the Meta WhatsApp Business API and Twilio for automatic customer messages and operator alerts, and tested the endpoints.

Limits: The repository is private, because it is client work. I cannot share code, screenshots, the client's name or its customers' data, so this page describes the design and my part in it. No message volumes, response times, customer counts or uptime figures are claimed here. The results above describe what the platform does, not how fast or how widely it ran. I built it during an internship. The WhatsApp connection was a prototype that I tested endpoint by endpoint, so I cannot show that it served live customers or say how it has been run or changed since. Meta sets rules for business accounts and message templates, and they shape what any WhatsApp bot may send. A new project needs those approvals planned first.

Where this fits: Clinics and appointment-based businesses: Customers message on WhatsApp to ask about or change bookings. An AI agent answers in the background, the conversation is saved, and operators can be alerted. Online shops and delivery firms: Customers ask where an order is or how to return it. The agent replies without making them wait and keeps the full history for support staff to read. Training and education providers: Learners ask about fees, timetables and enrolment on WhatsApp. An agent replies in the background and remembers each learner across sessions, and operators can be alerted. Small support teams with one WhatsApp number: The same questions arrive all day. An AI agent handles the routine ones while operators can be alerted for the cases you define.

Role: Internship project at Shivohini Tech-AI, built for a client.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Answers from your documents; A hand-over inbox for staff; Tracing and monitoring; Load test and message figures.

Q: How does the platform reply on WhatsApp without making customers wait? A: The receiver tracks the user and hands the AI work to a background queue (Redis and Celery). A worker writes the reply, and it goes back to the customer when it is ready. The web request that received the message is not held up by the AI, so a slow answer never blocks the next customer's message.

Q: What is a webhook in a WhatsApp automation? A: A webhook is a web address on your server that the messaging platform calls each time something happens, such as a customer sending a message. The platform pushes the message to you instead of you asking for it. Here a FastAPI endpoint received each message this way, then tracked the user and queued the AI work.

Q: How does the platform remember each customer's conversation? A: It stores each user's state and the full conversation history in PostgreSQL. When a new message arrives, the platform matches it to the right user and brings back their context, so the AI agent can carry on across sessions instead of starting again. The database, not the program's memory, holds the record.

Q: Do human operators get alerts from the platform? A: Yes. The platform connected the Meta WhatsApp Business API and Twilio for automatic customer messages and for alerts to human operators. Which situations should alert a person is a business rule. For a new project, that list would be agreed first, before building anything.

Q: Can I see the code for this WhatsApp project? A: No. It was a client project built during an internship, and the repository is private, so I cannot share the code, screenshots or the client's name. I can explain the design in an interview or on a call, and I can build something similar from scratch with its own accounts and data.

Q: What should I prepare before building a WhatsApp AI agent? A: Prepare the questions customers ask most, the cases that need a person, and who should receive alerts. You also need a WhatsApp Business account. Account approval and message templates are set on Meta's side, so ask early, because they shape what the bot may send and how soon it can start.

# Deepfake video detection project
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/deepfake-video-detection/
Case study: a small neural network scores each video frame as real or fake, with a Streamlit app, confidence chart and PDF report. 74.16% test accuracy.

This deepfake video detection project is a college team project. A small neural network scores every frame of an uploaded video as real or fake. A Streamlit web app shows a confidence chart and exports a PDF report. It reached 74.16% test accuracy on a random frame split. Co-built with Prasanna Patil and a classmate.

Newsrooms, banks that check identity on video, hiring teams and online platforms may receive video that has been altered. A face-swap clip can mislead an audience, pass a video identity check or damage a person's name. Reviewers who check every clip by eye cannot keep up, so they need a fast first filter that shows what to inspect.

A useful result is a first check, not a verdict. It scores a clip, shows which frames raised the score and produces a report a reviewer can file with the case. It also states how it was tested and where it fails, so that nobody mistakes a screening tool for proof.

Problem: Face-swap videos are hard to spot by eye, so reviewers need a quick, explainable first check. Without one, every clip needs careful manual review, and a fake that slips through can reach the news, a customer identity check or a hiring process. A bare yes or no also cannot be explained to a manager or a customer.

What made it hard: Faint traces of a face swap. A good swap leaves only faint traces, such as small texture and colour mismatches around the face. A small model has to learn to spot them in single frames. Near-identical frames. The first ten frames of a video look almost the same. A random split can put near copies in both training and test data, which can flatter the accuracy. Limited computing resources. The team's report says limited computing resources restrict training depth. The model is small and trains for 5 epochs, and the app scores each frame of an upload one at a time. Explaining the verdict. A reviewer needs more than the word "Fake". The app shows a score for every frame, a chart over the clip and a plain reading of the score bands, and the PDF keeps a record.

Approach: The team trained the model on Celeb-DF, a public set of real and face-swapped videos. The first ten frames of each video are resized to 224 by 224 pixels and varied slightly with small shifts, zooms and flips. A small three-block neural network (a CNN, a model type for images) learns from the training split of 7,856 frames to give each frame a real-or-fake score. A six-page Streamlit app lets a reviewer upload a video. It scores every frame, averages the scores into a Real or Fake verdict, charts the score per frame and explains the score bands. A PDF report can be downloaded.

My part: Worked as one of three members of a college team that built the detector, the Streamlit app and the written project report. Shared the work with Prasanna Patil and a classmate. The team's report does not record who did which part, so I claim no single module. Published the repository from my account, with the training notebook, the app code and an early draft of the report. The final 31-page report is not in the repository.

Context: The dataset, Celeb-DF, is a public research set of real and face-swapped videos. The model is a small CNN trained from scratch, not a pretrained network. The README describes ResNeXt and LSTM models, and the How It Works picture adds face detection and cropping. The code has only the small CNN, and this page follows the code. It is a college prototype that runs locally in Streamlit. No public demo is linked, and the Feedback page does not store anything.

Architecture: Data: Celeb-DF videos from the Celeb-real and YouTube-real folders are labelled real, those from Celeb-synthesis fake. The first ten frames of each video are resized to 224 by 224 pixels and split 80 to 20 at random, giving 7,856 training frames in the notebook's latest run.; Augmentation: training frames are varied slightly with rotation up to 10 degrees, small shifts, shear, zoom and horizontal flips. Test frames are only scaled to a 0 to 1 range, so the test is not changed by augmentation.; Model: a small three-block CNN. Three convolution layers of 32, 64 and 128 filters, each followed by pooling, then a dense layer of 64 units and a single 0 to 1 output (a sigmoid). It has about 5.6 million parameters and trains for 5 epochs with the Adam optimiser.; Verdict: each frame gets a score from 0 to 1. The app's confidence score is the mean of all frame scores as a percentage, and above 50 is Fake. It reads the bands as above 80 high confidence of a deepfake, 50 to 80 moderate, below 50 appears genuine.; App: a six-page Streamlit app with Home, Upload Video, Detection Results, How It Works, Feedback and About pages. It accepts mp4, mov, avi and mpeg files, previews the upload, scores every frame and draws a frame-by-frame chart of the scores.; Report: ReportLab builds a PDF with the video name, verdict, score, a reading guide for the bands and the first 40 frame scores.; Model delivery: the saved model file is fetched from Google Drive with gdown and cached by Streamlit, because the README treats a file over 25 MB as too big to upload..

Design decisions: A small CNN on single frames. The team trained a small three-block CNN on single frames, which its report records as a 3-layer ConvNet with augmentation and a sigmoid output. A small model trains with limited computing resources, which the report cites as a constraint, and it is simple to explain. The result is modest accuracy: 74.16%, which the report calls room for improvement. Score every frame, then average. The app scores every frame of an upload, averages the scores into one verdict and plots the score of each frame. The chart shows which parts of a clip drove the verdict, so a reviewer can check those frames by eye. The average keeps the final answer simple. Plain bands for the score. The app turns the average into three messages: above 80 high confidence of a deepfake, 50 to 80 moderate, below 50 appears genuine. The PDF repeats this guide. A reviewer who is not a data scientist can act on a band. The cut-offs are fixed numbers, not calibrated probabilities, so they guide attention and prove nothing. Celeb-DF and a random frame split. Training used Celeb-DF, which the report calls a clean dataset, with a random 80 to 20 split of frames and a fixed seed so runs can be repeated. One public dataset and a fixed seed keep the work repeatable. The trade-off is optimistic testing, because frames from one video can land on both sides, which a split by video would avoid.

Results: 74.16% test accuracy on a random 20% share of frames held out from training, measured by the notebook's evaluate step. The team's own report lists this as room for improvement.; 7,856 training frames of 224 by 224 pixels, from the first ten frames of each video in the Celeb-DF folders used. The saved model has about 5.6 million parameters, counted from the model file.; An end-to-end flow from upload to scoring, chart and PDF report in the app code, with screenshots of the upload, results and chart pages in the team's report.; The PDF report lists the verdict, the score, a reading guide for the bands and the first 40 frame scores.; A 31-page project report with requirements, a risk table, a project plan and a literature survey of four papers..

Limits: The 74.16% comes from a random split of frames, so frames of one video can sit in both training and test data. It likely flatters results on new videos, and the notebook gives no split of missed fakes and false alarms. The model looks at whole frames, not cropped faces, and learned from the first ten frames of Celeb-DF videos only. The team's report says it is limited to videos like Celeb-DF and does not cover audio fakes. The notebook's saved outputs come from different runs. The accuracy printout and the cell that shows 7,856 training frames were not run together, so treat them as the team's reported numbers, not one clean experiment. The app saves each upload to a temporary file and does not remove it, and its score is an average of frame scores, not a calibrated probability. Treat the result as a first check for a reviewer, not as proof.

Where this fits: Newsrooms and fact-checkers: Triage submitted clips so a person looks first at those the tool flags, and sees which frames drove the score before deciding, once accuracy is measured on the newsroom's own clips. Banks and onboarding teams: Test a first check on customer video, such as an identity check, and hand flagged cases to a trained reviewer with a report, once accuracy is measured on the bank's own videos. Hiring and HR teams: Test a first screen of recorded interview videos for signs of face swapping, with the report attached for a reviewer, once accuracy is measured on the team's own videos. Platforms that moderate uploads: Queue uploaded clips by suspicion score so human moderators check the highest scores first, once accuracy is measured on the platform's own videos.

Role: Member of a three-person college team. The repository is published from my account.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): A stronger model that watches across frames; Fairer testing by video; Face finding and cropping; Batch scoring API; Visual explanations.

Q: What is deepfake detection? A: Deepfake detection is software that checks whether a video has been faked, for example by swapping one person's face onto another. This project scores each frame as real or fake and combines the scores into a verdict. It is a first check for reviewers, not proof, because its accuracy is 74.16%.

Q: How can you detect a deepfake video? A: Use software as a first check and a person for the final call. This project resizes frames and scores each one with a small neural network. It averages the scores into Real or Fake and shows a confidence chart per frame. With 74.16% accuracy it points a reviewer where to look, and it cannot settle the question.

Q: How accurate is the detector? A: The notebook reports 74.16% on a random 20% share of Celeb-DF frames held out from training, so it is right about three times in four. Frames of one video can sit on both sides of the split, so results on new videos may be lower. The team's report lists it as room for improvement.

Q: Who worked on it? A: A three-person college team: Prasanna Patil, a classmate and me. The repository is published from my account. The team's report does not record who did which part, so I describe it as shared work rather than claiming a particular module as mine.

Q: Does the detector find and crop faces first? A: No. The model sees the whole frame, resized to 224 by 224 pixels, with no face detection or cropping in the code. The README describes a ResNeXt and LSTM design (an image network plus a sequence model) and an app diagram shows face cropping, but the code builds neither. A face detector is an extension I can add.

Q: What data was the model trained on? A: Celeb-DF, a public deepfake dataset. Videos in its Celeb-real and YouTube-real folders are labelled real, and the Celeb-synthesis folder is labelled fake. The first ten frames of each video were resized to 224 by 224 pixels and split 80 to 20 at random, which gave 7,856 training frames. Training added small shifts, zooms and flips.

Q: Can I use this as proof that a video is fake? A: No. It is a first-check tool with 74.16% accuracy on one dataset, and its score is an average of frame scores, not a calibrated probability. The team's report says the tool is meant for education and not for public accusation. Use it to decide which clips a person should examine closely.

# SMS spam classifier project built with Naive Bayes
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/spam-classifier/
SMS spam classifier project: TF-IDF and Naive Bayes on 5,169 text messages. 97.1% accuracy and no false alarms on 1,034 test messages.

This SMS spam classifier project is a small, early-stage build from an AICTE internship on AI. Using TF-IDF word scores and Naive Bayes, it labels a text message as spam or not spam. Built from 5,169 labelled messages, it scored 97.1% accuracy with no false alarms on 1,034 test messages, and a Streamlit page shows the label.

Teams that handle many incoming messages, such as a support desk or a shared inbox, lose time to spam, and scam messages put customers at risk. A trained text model can screen messages before a person reads them, so staff spend their time on the genuine ones. The harder part is doing that without hiding a message someone needs.

A good result is a filter that rarely blocks a genuine message, says how many spam messages it still misses, and can be retrained on a team's own labelled messages. This project is a small first version of that: a cleaned dataset, a measured model and a page where anyone can paste a message and see the label.

Problem: Spam text messages waste time and carry scams. Checking each one by hand does not scale, and a filter that wrongly blocks a genuine message does more harm than one that misses a few spam messages, because the reader never sees what was blocked. The aim was to teach a small model to tell the two apart, and to measure how often it makes each kind of mistake.

What made it hard: Few spam examples. Only 653 of the 5,169 cleaned messages, about 13%, are spam. A model can look accurate by calling everything genuine, so accuracy alone says little. Messy message text. Messages use abbreviations, numbers, symbols and odd spelling. The raw file also had 403 repeated messages and three mostly empty extra columns. All of it needed cleaning before any model could learn from it. Blocking a real message. A false alarm hides a genuine message from its reader, which costs more than a missed spam. The model had to be judged on both kinds of mistake, not on one score. Same cleaning in the page. The page must clean a pasted message exactly as the training messages were cleaned. Any difference would mean scoring words the model never saw, and the measured results would no longer apply.

Approach: Following a public tutorial, I started from a labelled collection of 5,572 text messages and removed 403 repeats, which left 5,169. I cleaned each message with NLTK: lowercase, split into words, keep letters and digits, drop very common words and cut words to their roots. TF-IDF then scored the 3,000 most frequent words, and a Multinomial Naive Bayes model learned from a random 80% of the messages. I tested it on the other 20%, 1,034 messages, and saved the model and word scores to files. A Streamlit page and a command-line script load those files, repeat the same cleaning and show Spam or Not Spam.

My part: The data work: dropping the empty columns, removing 403 repeated messages, and charts of class balance, message length and common words. Running the cleaning, TF-IDF word scoring and Naive Bayes steps on the data, with one 80/20 split to measure accuracy, precision and recall. The saved model and word-score files, so the page and the script use exactly what was tested. Setting up a Streamlit page taken from a public tutorial app, and writing predict.py, a command-line script, to label a pasted message as Spam or Not Spam. The formal project report for the programme, with screenshots of the page labelling one spam and one genuine message.

Context: Built for the AICTE internship on AI, delivered with TechSaksham, a Microsoft and SAP CSR initiative, under the programme's project guide. I was the only author. The messages are the public SMS Spam Collection. The page, the cleaning, the model comparison and the Naive Bayes steps follow a widely shared public tutorial project. It is an early-stage build and a local demo, not a production filter. The longer working notebook that compared other models is not in the public repository.

Architecture: A file of 5,572 labelled text messages. Three mostly empty extra columns were dropped and 403 repeated messages removed, leaving 5,169: 4,516 genuine and 653 spam.; Each message is made lowercase and split into words with NLTK (a Python toolkit for text). Punctuation and symbols are dropped, very common words (stop words) are removed, and words are cut to their roots with the Porter stemmer, so loving becomes love.; A TF-IDF vectoriser (scikit-learn) keeps the 3,000 most frequent words and scores each one by how often it appears in a message and how rare it is across all messages.; A Multinomial Naive Bayes classifier, a simple method that compares how often each word appears in spam and in genuine messages, with default settings. It learns from a random 80% of the messages (4,135); the other 20% (1,034) is kept for testing, split once with a fixed seed.; On the 1,034 test messages the confusion matrix shows all 896 genuine messages passed, 108 of 138 spam messages caught and 30 missed. That gives accuracy 97.10%, precision 100% and recall 78.26%.; The trained word scores and model are saved as two pickle files (Python's way of storing objects), each under 100 KB, so the page and the script load exactly what was tested.; A Streamlit page titled Email/SMS Spam Classifier, though only text messages were used, has a text box and a Predict button and shows Spam or Not Spam. A command-line script, predict.py, does the same for one message. Both repeat the cleaning steps first..

Design decisions: Remove repeats before splitting. I removed 403 repeated messages before splitting the data, rather than leaving them in. A message that appears in both the training and test sets would be recognised, not judged, and would lift the score. Removing repeats first keeps the test fairer. Put precision first. In the model comparison I ranked models by precision and kept one that blocked no genuine message, over several with higher accuracy. A blocked genuine message is lost without its reader knowing, while a missed spam is only an annoyance. Precision and recall are reported next to accuracy because accuracy alone hides this. Multinomial Naive Bayes over other models. Following a public tutorial, I kept Multinomial Naive Bayes after a longer working notebook scored 14 other models and combinations on the same split, including Bernoulli Naive Bayes (98.4% accuracy, 1 false alarm). Only it and nearest-neighbour search flagged no genuine message, and it was far more accurate than that one (97.1% against 90.5%). The saved model is also small, under 100 KB. Save the model, reuse the cleaning. I saved the trained word scores and model to files and repeated the exact cleaning steps in the page, rather than retraining or cleaning differently when the page starts. The page always uses the exact objects that were tested, and a pasted message is cleaned like the training messages, so the measured scores still apply.

Results: 97.10% accuracy on 1,034 test messages, a random 20% of the cleaned data, measured once in the notebook.; 100% precision: none of the 896 genuine test messages was flagged as spam, so there were no false alarms.; 78.26% recall: 108 of the 138 spam messages in the test set were caught and 30 were missed.; A filter that never flagged anything would still score 86.7% on this test set, because 896 of its 1,034 messages are genuine. That is why precision and recall are reported next to accuracy.; In the longer working notebook, 15 models and combinations were scored on the same split. Only two flagged no genuine message, and this one was the more accurate of the two.; The formal project report gives no accuracy number, so every figure on this page comes from the notebook output..

Limits: Text messages only, in one language. No email was used for training or testing, so email accuracy is unknown. Emails are longer and carry subjects, links and attachments, so an email filter would need its own labelled data. One dataset, one random split. The test result is a single measurement, and the word scores were learned from all messages before the split, so the figure is slightly optimistic. Newer scam wording would need fresh data. It misses about one spam message in five (30 of 138 on the test set). A real filter would need a cut-off the owner can tune, a review folder for flagged messages and regular retraining on new messages. It is a local demo: no automated tests, no monitoring, no link to any messaging system, and the requirements file pins older library versions than the ones that saved the model files.

Where this fits: Support desks and shared inboxes: A team that reads many incoming messages could screen out likely spam first and send it to a review folder instead of deleting it, so genuine requests are not lost. Businesses that text their customers: A company that sends and receives customer texts could flag scam or junk messages before staff or customers act on them, once the model is retrained on its own labelled messages. Community and marketplace moderators: A site with user messages or comments needs a first pass that flags promotions and scams for a person to confirm. A model retrained on the site's own labelled examples can supply it. Telecom and messaging product teams: The project report names messaging apps and telecom services as places a filter could sit. A team there could use this build as a starting point and test it on its own traffic.

Role: Sole author (20 commits), following a public tutorial, under the programme's project guide.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Retraining on your own messages; Adjustable cut-off and review queue; Prediction API; Comparison with stronger language models; Feedback from reviewers.

Q: How does a spam classifier for text messages work? A: A spam classifier turns a message into numbers and lets a trained model decide whether it looks like spam. Here the text is cleaned, each word is scored with TF-IDF, and a Naive Bayes model, trained on 4,135 of 5,169 labelled text messages, answers Spam or Not Spam.

Q: How accurate is this spam classifier? A: On 1,034 held-out text messages it scored 97.10% accuracy, 100% precision and 78.26% recall: no genuine message was flagged and 30 of 138 spam messages were missed. It is one random split of one dataset, so new messages, other languages or email could score differently.

Q: What do precision and recall mean for spam? A: Precision is the share of flagged messages that were truly spam. Recall is the share of all spam that was found. Here, on the test set, precision is 100%, so no genuine message was flagged, and recall is 78.26%, so about one spam message in five got through. A useful filter needs both numbers, not accuracy alone.

Q: Did you compare Naive Bayes with other models? A: The notebook in the public repository trains only Multinomial Naive Bayes. A longer working notebook, kept outside the repository, scored 15 models and combinations on the same split. Only two flagged no genuine message, and I kept Naive Bayes because it was the more accurate of those two.

Q: Can this spam classifier filter my company's email? A: Not as it stands. It learned from text messages only, so email was never tested. For email I would collect labelled examples of your own mail, retrain the model and measure precision and recall on messages it has not seen, before any message is blocked automatically.

Q: Is the spam classifier ready for production? A: No. It is an early-stage project built for an internship programme: one dataset, one test split and a local demo page. A production filter also needs fresh data, regular retraining, monitoring, a review queue for flagged messages and automated tests. I can build those around the model.

Q: Where did the spam classifier project come from? A: I was the only author, with 20 commits. It was the project for the AICTE internship on AI delivered with TechSaksham, a Microsoft and SAP CSR initiative, under the programme's project guide. It follows a public tutorial, and it was submitted with a formal report that gives no accuracy figure.

# AI engineer portfolio projects and case studies
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/
Selected AI chatbot, computer vision, speech and Python backend projects by Shaunak Chorge, with case studies, results and the tools behind each one.

These are the AI engineer portfolio projects I have worked on so far. They show the AI systems I built for audit and compliance features, conversational AI that cites its sources, a backend that traces slow requests, and speech, vision and automation work. Each case study covers the problem, what I built, the results and what I can add next.

Answers grounded in documents: Staff and customers need quick answers from long policies and regulations, with the source shown. The healthcare chatbot cites its source or says "not found", and the obligation system lists the duties in a regulation, each linked to its passage.

AI output a regulated team can check: In audit, compliance and banking, an answer is only useful if it can be verified. These projects block invented figures in code, attach a source quote to every duty and score generated queries by running them.

Watching cameras and video: Teams cannot watch every camera or check every clip by eye. The CCTV prototype turns a camera feed into crowd alerts, possible-crime labels and saved evidence. The deepfake checker, a college team project, scores a video frame by frame for face-swap manipulation.

Sorting voice and text with trained models: When there are too many recordings or messages to read, a trained model can sort them. The speech model reads mood from voice clips and the spam filter flags unwanted messages, and each states how its accuracy was tested.

Automated chats and scam defence: Customers expect quick replies on WhatsApp, and a blocked scammer simply tries the next number. The WhatsApp platform answers with AI in the background and keeps each conversation's history. The honeypot keeps scammers talking and records their payment details.

AI backends that stay fast and traceable: An AI feature in use needs a backend that stays quick and can be explained when something goes wrong. The traceable backend follows each request with an ID, and the WhatsApp platform moves slow AI work to background jobs.

Q: What are some real world AI project examples? A: Real examples on this site include an AI that drafts audit findings from checklist notes, a text-to-SQL assistant for a bank database and a scam-catching AI honeypot. Each one has a case study with the problem, the build and the results.

Q: Which projects are client work and which are personal builds? A: The audit drafting, obligation extraction and text-to-SQL case studies are my recent work at Claptek. The others are internship work and personal or academic builds, including hackathon and assignment work. Every case study states its origin and my role, so you can see my own part in it.

Q: Why are the client projects described without names? A: Client work is confidential. The pages explain the problem, my part and the measured results without naming the client, the product or any internal system. I only name a client or show their work with written approval. Anything I cannot share, or cannot prove, stays off the page.

Q: Can I see the code behind these projects? A: Where a repository is public, the case study links to it. That includes the healthcare chatbot, the honeypot, the CCTV prototype and the speech, deepfake and spam builds. Client code and the traceable backend are private, so for those I explain the design, my part and the results instead.

Q: How do you separate what you built from what you adapted? A: Each case study lists what I did myself next to what already existed, such as a teammate's work, a public training recipe or earlier code. The speech model adapts a public recipe, and in the text-to-SQL work my teammate built the table search and the safety guard.

Q: Are the accuracy numbers on these pages from real tests? A: Yes. Each accuracy figure states how it was measured, for example a random test split, 1,034 test messages or queries run on a real database. Where a score is modest or has a caveat, the page says so next to the number. I do not add figures I cannot show.
